These updates are reflected in the revised version of Fig. 3f and the Source Data file. Comment 13: Fig5a and ED Fig 9a Conversely supplementation with IP , both in cells or extracts, 6 counteracted the UNI418-induced Cul4A neddylation (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 9a). The authors should present the results with supplementation with IP in absence of 6 UNI418 Response: As recommended, we recognized that the group treated with IP alone had not been 6 included in the original experiment. We therefore performed an additional set of experiments in which cells or extracts were treated with IP in the absence of UNI418, 6 with three independent biological replicates. The newly generated data (Fig. 5a and Extended data Fig. 9a) have been added to the revised figures and included in the Source Data file. Comment 14: Rephrase UNI418-mediated reduction in HR frequency, attributed to the proteolysis of HR proteins by activated Cul4A ubiquitin ligase following down-regulation of IP via 6 inhibition of PIKfyve/PIP5K1C by UNI418, was also restored upon additional supplementation of IP Rephrase! Suggestion. “UNI418-mediated reduction in HR 6 frequency was also restored upon additional supplementation of IP . 6 Response: As recommended, we have revised the sentence to the clearer phrasing: “UNI418-mediated reduction in HR frequency was also restored upon additional supplementation of IP .” This change has been incorporated into the revised manuscript. 6 Comment 15: IP6 toxicity However, it is important to note that IP exhibited toxicity in both WT and 6 parp1-/- cells. The authors may show in ED the data. Response: In our study, IP supplementation was performed as a brief 10-minute treatment. The 6 goal of IP6 supplementation in our assays was to transiently restore intracellular IP 6 levels rather than to maintain long-term IP elevation, which is typically associated with 6 cytotoxic effects. For this reason, cytotoxicity was not expected in our experimental setup. We have added a clarifying statement in the revised manuscript to explain why toxicity was not assessed in this context. Comment 16: Partial knockdown In contrast, WDR5 knockdown did not increase CtIP levels (data not shown). The authors mention here and elsewhere “knockdown” of proteins while the levels of the proteins upon siRNA treatments are only weakened. They should precise and comment the potential impact of residual levels of the proteins. Response: As described in the manuscript, our screening strategy was designed to identify the DCAF responsible for RAD51 proteolysis. Based on the established role of DCAFs in determining Cul4A substrate specificity, we screened more than 60 predicted DCAFs using siRNAs and monitored RAD51 and CHK1 levels. WDR5 was the only candidate whose silencing consistently increased both proteins, and we therefore focused our analysis on WDR5 as the relevant DCAF. WDR5 was identified through screening with RAD51 and CHK1 as readouts. However, WDR5 knockdown shows minimal or no effect on CtIP, which is likely regulated by a different DCAF or degradation pathway. We commented it in the revised manuscript. Furthermore, to assess whether residual protein levels from partial knockdown may influence the results, we performed experiments under MG132 treatment, which fully blocks proteolysis. Under these conditions, the effects of WDR5 and CUL4A knockdown were further enhanced, supporting the conclusion that the observed phenotypes were indeed limited by the presence of residual protein. We commented it in the revised manuscript. “In contrast, WDR5 knockdown did not increase CtIP levels (data not shown), which suggest CtIP is regulated by other DCAF. Additional proteasome inhibition using MG132 showed further enhancement of the observed effects, suggesting that residual protein levels due to incomplete knockdown of WDR5 and CUL4A may have masked the full recovery of RAD51 and CHK1 (data not shown).” This figure is not included in the revised manuscript. It is only for reviewers. Comment 17: Fig. 6d, the authors should add the level of RFWD3 in presence of siRNA. Response: To examine RFWD3 levels upon siRNA treatment, we purchased the commercially available antibody cited in previously published studies and performed immunoblotting. However, the antibody did not yield a detectable or specific signal under our experimental conditions, making it difficult to reliably assess RFWD3 protein levels. As an alternative, we measured RFWD3 mRNA expression by qPCR, and these results were added to Extended Data Fig. 9g in the revised manuscript. Comment 18: Combined use of UNI418 and Oliparib Crucially, this increase in drug sensitivity was paralleled by a marked elevation in apoptotic cell death among the PARPi resistant C4-2 cells following UNI418 treatment The effect is less significative with combined use of UNI418 and Oliparib. The authors may indicate and comment. Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue. Upon careful re-examination of the data used in the original submission, we identified an error in the dataset associated with the apoptotic cell death analysis in the combination treatment condition. This error affected the apparent magnitude of the effect observed with the combined use of UNI418 and Olaparib. We have now corrected the dataset, re-plotted the graphs, and re-performed the statistical analyses using the corrected values. Following this correction, the revised data accurately reflect the effects of UNI418 alone and in combination with Olaparib in PARPi- resistant C4-2 cells. The updated figures and statistical analyses have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Fig. 7i). We apologize for any confusion caused by the initial error and appreciate the reviewer’s careful assessment, which helped us improve the accuracy and clarity of the presented data. Comment 19: Redundancy End of results part and beginning of discussion are redundant. Response: We agree that the opening statement of the Discussion section partially overlapped with the concluding paragraph of the Results. To address this redundancy, we have removed the overlapping explanatory sentences from the beginning of the Discussion and reorganized the opening paragraph to ensure that the Discussion section no longer repeats information presented in the Results. Reviewer #2 Comment 1: Data transparency – To facilitate data transparency, I suggest the authors show individual data points on all graphs so that readers get a better sense of the data distribution in experiments. Response: In accordance with the recommendation, we have revised all graphs throughout the manuscript to display individual data points. These updated figures are included in the revised manuscript. Comment 2: Western blot quantification – The authors mention several times that protein levels are significantly or substantially changed between different treatment conditions, but do not consistently present quantified data of relevant immunoblots supported with statistical tests to back up these otherwise only qualitative claims. I recommend that the authors include relevant quantifications of immunoblot data (where these claims are directed) to better support any assertions. The use of superlatives to describe changes should also be limited and/or fully removed, as these have limited quantitative meaning. Response: To address this concern, we have now included quantitative analyses for the key immunoblot data supporting our conclusions. For the relevant experiments, three independent biological replicates were performed, and representative full immunoblot images from all repeats have been provided in the Source Data files. Band intensities were quantified using ImageJ, and values were normalized to the appropriate loading controls (α-tubulin, GAPDH, or histone H3, as indicated for each experiment). The normalized values are now displayed numerically above each corresponding band in the figures. Comment 3: DNA Replication Stress Response – In figure 1, the authors measure DNA replication stress response suppression by induction of ATAD5. I am wondering how inhibition by the two small molecule inhibitors compares to inhibition of CHK1 phosphorylation via ATR inhibition, as that could be a good positive control for suppression of certain facets of the DNA replication stress response. Response: To address this point, we incorporated ATR inhibitor (ATRi) as a positive control for suppression of the DNA replication stress response. In the revised figure, we now directly compare each treatment condition individually—ML367, UNI418, and ATRi—by examining their respective effects on p-CHK1 and total CHK1 levels. Comment 4: DNA replication stress response inhibition – Induction of ATAD5 between ML367 and UNI418 are different in figure 1C, making it difficult to make any comparison about suppression of DNA replication stress response as currently presented in the manuscript. Another interpretation could be that both inhibitors function similarly as they both result in ~75% reduction in signals at the highest concentration of inhibitors. Furthermore, the authors do not make any comparisons between dissociation constants or IC between 50 ML367 and UNI418 in the text, which would allow readers to draw conclusions about whether UNI418 displays heightened suppression of the DNA replication stress response. I suggest the authors make mention of these values to support their claims. Response: Thanks for the comment. To clarify the relative effects of ML367 and UNI418 on the DNA replication stress response, we examined the quantitative values provided in the Source Data for ATAD5 luciferase activity. At the highest concentration tested (5 µM), ML367 reduced ATAD5 luciferase activity by approximately 70% compared to the 5-FUrd–treated control, whereas UNI418 reduced the signal by approximately 90% under the same conditions. These measurements indicate a substantially stronger suppression of replication stress signaling by UNI418 relative to ML367. To facilitate interpretation of these differences, we have updated Fig. 1c to report the IC values for ATAD5 luciferase activity, which further substantiates the conclusion that 50 UNI418 more potently suppresses the replication stress response. Comment 5: RAD51 Foci quantification in Figure 3 – please describe if this was done manually or whether an automated foci detection system was used. If the latter was used, please provide a brief description of the pipeline in the methods section. a. It is also important to understand whether cells in G2 phase were distinguished from cells in S-phase (at the time of irradiation / analysis of foci), as DSB repair processes between each phase are distinct. In the context of this work, selective analysis of cells irradiated in S-phase and analyzed in S-phase would be most logical. b. The legends indicate that these cells were monitored 1 hour after 10 Gy, a dose and time point that I am honestly very surprised that “only” an average of ~15 RAD51 foci are observed in the control / DMSO. From experience and understanding of comparable literature, foci numbers at least twice this are anticipated, as 10 Gy would be predicted to induce 100-200 DNA breaks in a G1 phase cell and 200-400 breaks in a G2 phase cell (with intermediate numbers in S-phase) depending on cell type genome content. While not all IR-induced breaks will undergo HR and form RAD51, at least 1/3 of induced breaks at any given time are expected to. It is not uncommon for radiation dosimetry here to vary substantially between groups if irradiator calibration is not up-to-date, or it could be possible that too many breaks are occurring and challenging for the authors to separate (foci are merging). I would advise the authors to examine this issue more closely in the context of what is understood from the published literature, as these numbers do appear far less than expected for that dose. c. Finally, while Figure 3b is helpful, it is a single time point and understanding whether the UNI418 specific effect is transient by performing a few timepoints in addition to the 1h would be helpful. Response: Thanks for the comment. RAD51 foci were quantified using confocal microscopy followed by semi-automated analysis in ZEN software (Carl Zeiss). Images were acquired on an LSM880 confocal microscope using identical acquisition settings for all samples. After background subtraction, nuclei were segmented based on DAPI, and RAD51 foci were quantified exclusively in EdU-positive nuclei, which had been identified following Click-iT detection. Foci were detected using the ZEN spot detection module with fixed thresholding parameters applied uniformly across all samples. Quantification was performed on ≥50 EdU-positive nuclei per condition. These details have been added to the Methods section. To address reviewer’s comment, we redid experiments several times more after recalibrating our x-ray machine. a. To address concerns regarding cell-cycle heterogeneity, we restricted our analysis to S-phase cells identified by EdU incorporation. Cells were pulse-labeled with EdU after irradiation, followed by Click-iT detection immediately prior to imaging. Only EdU-positive nuclei were included in the RAD51 foci quantification. This clarification has been added to Fig. 3b. b. b. In our repeated experiments, S-phase cells exhibited an average of more than 30 RAD51 foci at the 1 h time point. Reported values in the literature vary substantially depending on cell type, irradiation conditions, and quantification methods, ranging widely from ~20 to >80 foci. Therefore, the values observed in our experiments fall within the variability reported across published studies. c. In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we examined RAD51 foci at 1 h, 3 h, and 6 h after irradiation. The suppressive effect of UNI418 on RAD51 foci was observed at all timepoints, indicating that the effect is not transient. Comment 6: DSB Repair Efficiency – In figure 3F, the authors show both a large reduction in HR efficiency and a small reduction in NHEJ efficiency when cells are treated with UNI418 in the I-Sce1 plasmid reporter assay. Testing whether the repair of genomic breaks by monitoring foci numbers in G1, S, and G2 cells over a time course following some other form of genotoxic stress would further support the claims of reduced repair efficiency and validate the observations with the plasmid-based assay, which are otherwise not able to distinguish effects between phases. HU, IR, ATR inhibitors, Camptothecin, or even endogenous DNA replication stress might be used in this context – with the most important thing being to monitor damage formed and resolved in S-phase separately from other phases. Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion. We fully agree that monitoring DSB repair kinetics in G1, S, and G2 cells following genotoxic stress would provide additional mechanistic insight. However, performing a full cell-cycle–resolved time-course analysis using multiple markers (γH2AX, 53BP1, RAD51) is beyond the scope and technical feasibility of the current revision timeline. Importantly, our study already incorporates several complementary assays that directly assess HR repair efficiency in S-phase cells: • EdU-based RAD51 foci quantification (Fig. 3b), • I-SceI DR-GFP reporter assay (Fig. 3e), • Effects of UNI418 on replication-stress–induced DDR signaling (Fig. 1), all of which consistently demonstrate that UNI418 markedly reduces HR activity. While we agree that additional time-course experiments could provide further detail, the combined results from our existing assays robustly support the conclusion that UNI418 impairs HR-mediated DSB repair. Comment 7: Synthetic lethality with Olaparib – it would be interesting to see how cell survival in the combination treatment compares to cell survival when BRCA1 or BRCA2 are knocked down by siRNA, as this is the canonical example of synthetic lethality in DNA repair. Response: To address this point, we performed additional experiments using siBRCA2 as HR- deficient control (Fig. 4d). As expected, BRCA2 knockdown increased sensitivity to olaparib, serving as a canonical HR-deficient reference. Notably, the extent of viability reduction observed upon dual depletion of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C was comparable to that seen with BRCA2 knockdown. Comment 8: PARPi resistance and re-sensitization – In Figure 7, the authors examine PARPi resistance by BRCA2 reversion, but there are quite a few known and different mechanisms that cells (especially cancer cells) can leverage to become more resistant to PARPi action. It would be interesting to see whether BRCA1/2 negative cells that have restored homologous recombination repair due to TP53BP1 loss, or resistance due to increased efflux pump expression, are re-sensitized to PARPi when treated with UNI418. Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion. We fully agree that PARP inhibitor resistance can arise through multiple mechanisms, including TP53BP1 loss–mediated restoration of HR and drug efflux pump upregulation. Testing whether UNI418 re- sensitizes such models would indeed provide additional mechanistic insight. However, generating or obtaining TP53BP1-deficient BRCA1/2 mutant lines or efflux pump–overexpressing PARPi-resistant models, and validating their resistance mechanisms, is beyond the scope and technical feasibility of the current revision timeline. We will evaluate whether UNI418 could restore PARPi sensitivity to other types of resistant mechanisms in future study. Importantly, our study already demonstrates that UNI418 re-sensitizes PARPi-resistant cells driven by BRCA2 reversion, a clinically relevant resistance mechanism. Together with the consistent HR suppression shown in multiple independent assays (RAD51 foci, DR-GFP reporter, DDR signaling), our results strongly support the conclusion that UNI418 enhances PARPi sensitivity by targeting HR restoration. Comment 9: Big Picture – It is not clear within the discussion whether the authors think that their tool compounds can be modified for therapeutic purposes, and this would be helpful. I was also expecting some discussion about differences in IP and related biosynthetic 6 processes between normal and cancer cells, and between different cancer types that naturally would have plenty of metabolic variation given their context and specific genomic profile. Response: To address these points, we expanded the Discussion to incorporate broader therapeutic implications of UNI418 and to introduce biological differences in IP metabolism relevant 6 to cancer contexts. Specifically, we added a paragraph that discusses cancer-type– associated variation in IP biosynthetic enzymes and their potential influence on tumor 6 biology and treatment vulnerability: “In addition to these mechanistic findings, accumulating evidence suggests that IP6 metabolism itself may differ across cancer types. While UNI418 does not directly target IP6K or IPMK, dysregulation of these upstream enzymes has been associated with tumor biology and clinical prognosis. IP6K2 functions as a tumor suppressor in breast cancer, whereas IP6K1 upregulation correlates with aggressive recurrence and poor survival outcomes. These data suggest that distinct nodes within the inositol phosphate network are differentially exploited by malignancies. Tumors heavily dependent on HR and IP6 metabolic wiring may therefore be uniquely vulnerable to agents—such as UNI418—that reduce cellular IP pools. Future comparative metabolomic and genomic analyses across 6 tumor lineages will be essential for defining biomarkers that predict UNI418 sensitivity and guide clinical application. Taken together, these findings establish a mechanistic link between inositol phosphate signaling, HR dependency, and exploitable therapeutic vulnerabilities in DNA repair–dependent cancers, including those with BRCA dysfunction or PARPi resistance.” Comment 10: “DNA repair” – throughout this manuscript, the words “DNA repair” are used to actually refer to “DNA double strand break repair” or similar. The processes being discussed here are specific to that type of DNA damage in the context of DNA replication, and not all possible types of DNA damage that exist. Please amend all instances of that language to be specific. Response: Thanks for thoughtful comments. We fully agree that the term “DNA repair” was at times used in a broad manner, whereas the processes discussed in our study relate specifically to DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair mechanisms, particularly those occurring during DNA replication. To address this, we carefully revised the manuscript to ensure that terminology is used with appropriate specificity throughout. In all relevant sections—Introduction, Results, and Discussion—we replaced general references to “DNA repair” with more accurate terms such as “DNA double-strand break repair,” “DSB repair,” or “HR-dependent DSB repair,” depending on the context. Comment 11: Western blot loading control –In figure 1b, the appropriate loading control for pRPA32 is total RPA32 levels, please include this control. H3 is less ideal in the context of that experiment. Response: We agree that total RPA32 serves as a more appropriate loading control for pRPA32 analysis. To address the reviewer’s request, we additionally treated cells with CPT and HU and examined CHK1, p-CHK1, p-RPA32, and total RPA32 levels. The results indicate that CHK1, p-CHK1, and p-RPA32 were reduced in ML367-treated cells and further decreased upon UNI418 treatment, whereas total RPA32 levels remained unchanged (Fig 1d, 1e). In Extended Fig. 1b, we showed that 5-FUrd treatment decreased p- CHK1 and CHK1 in ML367-treated cells and further reduced p-CHK1 and CHK1 in UNI418-treated cells. Comment 12: How these inhibitors are referred to – generally it is advisable to be specific and call them PARP1/2-trapping inhibitors, as other small molecules that block PARP enzyme action exist, with no to variable impact on trapping PARP enzymes at sites of DNA leading to damage. Response: We agree that the term “PARP inhibitors” can be ambiguous, as it encompasses both catalytic inhibitors and clinically used agents that induce PARP1/2 trapping. To address this, the sentence in the Introduction has been updated to: “The approval of clinically used PARP1/2-trapping inhibitors (commonly referred to as PARP inhibitors, PARPis), such as Olaparib, Niraparib, Rucaparib, Veliparib, and Talazoparib, by the US FDA, marks a pivotal advancement in the treatment of breast and ovarian cancers carrying BRCA mutations.” We have applied this terminology consistently throughout the revised manuscript. Comment 13: Data normalization –In Figure 1a, it is not clearly stated whether the Luc-ATAD5 data is normalized or not. The authors should revise all figures and clearly state whether the data is normalized, and if so, what the data is normalized to. Response: In Figure 1a, the Luc-ATAD5 activity was normalized to the NT (non-treated) control, which was set to 1, and all other values are presented as relative fold changes. We have now clarified this in the figure legend. We also carefully reviewed other figures and added explicit descriptions of normalization methods in the corresponding legends wherever necessary to ensure consistency and transparency in data presentation. Comment 14: Phosphorylation of CHK1 – I would suggest including the blot of phospho-CHK1 in the main body of the manuscript in figure 1. Response: In accordance with the comment, we have moved the phospho-CHK1 blot into the main Figure 1d. Additionally, based on comments from other reviewers, we repeated the experiments under multiple conditions, including ATR inhibitor treatment, to more comprehensively assess CHK1 phosphorylation dynamics. The revised figure now reflects these updated and expanded datasets. Comment 15: Kinase screen – I suggest the authors include extended data figure 2 in the main body as it guides the narrative of the study. I would also ask for more details on what precent control is referring to, and that the authors label the kinases of interest within the plot to make it more clear to the reader. Response: In accordance with the comment, the kinase screening data previously shown in Extended Data Fig. 2a has been moved into the main figure panel (now Fig. 2a) to better support the flow of the manuscript. To clarify the definition of “percent control,” we have added the following explanation in the figure: “Percent Control = (Signal with UNI418 / Signal with DMSO) × 100. Kinases showing 0 ≤ x < 10% control are highlighted (22 kinases in total).” We also considered highlighting or labeling the kinases of interest directly within the plot. However, due to the large number of kinases and the limited figure size, adding individual labels significantly reduced overall readability. Therefore, instead of labeling them within the plot, we have listed the names of the 22 kinases (0–10% control group) below the figure for clarity. Comment 16: Figure 2A is missing axis labels, please include these. Response: In the revised manuscript, we regenerated the graph using Prism to improve overall clarity and readability and added the appropriate axis labels. The updated graph is now presented as Fig. 2b. Comment 17: Surface plasmon resonance – In figure 2B, there is no description of what the black lines underneath the colored lines represent. Please describe what these are or remove them. Response: In Fig. 2b (now Fig. 2c), the black lines represent the predicted fitted curves generated from the kinetic binding model used for SPR analysis. We have added a clear explanation of this in the figure legend of the revised manuscript. “c, The kinase domains of MBP-tagged PIP5K1C and PIKfyve were immobilized to the CM5 chip. SPR was carried out after injecting UNI418. The black curves indicate the model-predicted fits corresponding to the experimental sensorgrams shown in color.” Comment 18: The methods section describes two cell viability assays, but it is not clear in the figure which one is used for each dataset. Please include this information within the appropriate figure legends. It is also not clear why two different cell viability assays need to be used Response: In our study, we used two complementary cell viability assays — the CellTiter-Glo assay and the clonogenic survival assay — to assess short-term metabolic viability and long- term proliferative capacity, respectively. We have now clearly indicated in each figure legend which assay was used for the corresponding dataset. Comment 19: Representative images of clonogenic cell survival assays – When appropriate, I would appreciate the if the authors included representative images of their cell survival assays, specifically clonogenic cell survival assays. Response: In accordance with the request, we have added representative images of the clonogenic survival assays to the revised manuscript (now included in Extended Data Fig. 8b). Comment 20: CUL4A neddylation – Figure 5a and 5b are missing a control that clearly demonstrates that the higher molecular weight CUL4A band is clearly CUL4A-Nedd. The authors should include a blot demonstrating that this band does not appear in the presence of an inhibitor of neddylation such as the compound MLN4924 used in reference 39. Response: In response, we performed additional experiments by including a treatment group with the neddylation inhibitor MLN4924. As shown in the revised figure, the higher–molecular weight CUL4A band disappears upon MLN4924 treatment, confirming that this band indeed represents the neddylated form of CUL4A. This new data has been added to the updated version of Fig. 5a. Comment 21: I would recommend the authors merge the graphs in extended data 9C and use dash lines to represent additional treatments. Response: As recommended, we have merged the graphs in Extended Data Fig. 9c and used dashed lines to represent the additional treatment conditions. These changes have been incorporated into the revised figure (now included in Extended Data Fig. 9c). Comment 22: IPPK siRNA – The authors did not include a control demonstrating the effectiveness of their siRNA against IPPK. Response: To address this concern, we performed RT–qPCR analysis to evaluate the knockdown efficiency of IPPK following siRNA treatment. The results confirming effective depletion of IPPK mRNA have been added to the revised manuscript (now included in Extended Data Fig. 9f). Comment 23: In figure 6C, the authors make the claim that silencing WDR or CUL4A causes resistance to Olaparib, but only shows comparison compared to vehicle controls. To support this claim, please show the results of the statistical test between the different siRNAs at 20 µM and 40 µM Olaparib. Response: In accordance with the suggestion, we have reanalyzed the data and performed statistical comparisons between the siRNA treatment groups (siWDR5 and siCUL4A) and the control siRNA at both 20 µM and 40 µM Olaparib. The updated statistical analyses are now reflected in the revised Fig. 6c, and the corresponding significance values have been added to the figure. Reviewer #3 and #4 Comment 1: The introduction should include the background of ATAD5. The authors state that ML367 was identified in 2010 and shown to increase ATAD5 protein levels under replication stress. Since UNI418 is a derivative of ML367, these facts, as well as the functional relevance of ATAD5 stabilization, should be included. Is it generally accepted that ATAD5 stabilization reflects replication stress? Response: In response, we have revised the Introduction to include background information regarding ATAD5 biology, its relevance to replication stress, and the historical connection between ML367 and UNI418. Specifically, we added the following paragraph to provide conceptual context: “ATAD5 (also known as ELG1 in yeast) is an essential PCNA unloader that maintains genome stability during DNA replication. Loss or depletion of ATAD5 results in persistent PCNA retention on chromatin, replication fork stalling, and elevated replication stress, ultimately contributing to genomic instability and tumorigenesis 19. Importantly, ATAD5- luciferase expression of the reporter cell line is markedly induced under replication stress, and this increase has been widely used as an established molecular marker for replication stress responses 20. In 2010, we reported that a small molecule ML367 selectively suppresses the elevation of ATAD5-luciferase protein levels in the reporter cell under replication stress conditions 21.” Comment 2: • The authors used 5-FU for 16–24 hours to induce replication stress. However, 5-FU is not a standard agent for inducing replication stress in cancer cells, and indeed pRPA32 was only modestly increased (Fig. 1d). Would similar results be obtained with other established replication stress inducers such as HU or camptothecin? • I recommend including supplementary data using alternative replication stress– inducing drugs to validate the conclusion that UNI418 represses replication stress. Response: We agree that 5-FUrd is not the most commonly used replication stress inducer and understand the reviewer’s concern regarding p-RPA32 signal intensity. In response, we performed additional experiments using two well-established replication stress agents, hydroxyurea (HU) and camptothecin (CPT). Cells were treated with HU or CPT, followed by ML367 or UNI418 exposure, and we examined CHK1, p-CHK1, p-RPA32, and total RPA32 levels. Consistent with our original 5-FUrd data, HU and CPT treatment revealed that CHK1, p-CHK1, and p-RPA32 were reduced by ML367 and further decreased by UNI418, while total RPA32 remained unchanged. These results confirm that UNI418 suppresses replication stress signaling across multiple replication-blocking agents. The newly obtained HU and CPT data have been incorporated as Fig. 1d and 1e in the revised manuscript. Comment 3: • In Fig. 1d and e, the blot for total RPA2 should be shown. The CHK1 blot from Extended Data Fig. 1b could be moved to the main figure because it is the key point of Figure 1. Response: Thanks for the suggestion. Fig. 1d and 1e are now presented with newly generated HU- and CPT-based replication stress experiments, and these panels include total RPA32 blots to provide appropriate loading controls. Regarding the CHK1 and p-CHK1 results originally shown in Extended Data Fig. 1b under 5-FUrd treatment, we retained these data in the extended section because HU and CPT experiments now occupy the corresponding position in the main figure panels. Therefore, the expanded CHK1 and p-CHK1 blots under 5-FUrd treatment are presented in the updated Extended Data Figure, while Figures 1d and 1e in the main manuscript focus on HU and CPT-based stress responses. Comment 4: • Fig. 2a: The x-axis should be annotated. Response: Sorry not to provide better graph in the original submission. We have improved the quality of Fig 2d (now Fig. 2b) by replacing the original graph which was provided by the company with a newly generated version using GraphPad Prism with actual dataset, which now includes clear X- and Y-axis labels, error ranges and higher graphical clarity. Comment 5: • Fig. 2d: The phosphatidylinositol pathway may be unfamiliar to many readers primarily interested in DNA damage responses and PARPi. A schematic explaining the relationships among PIKfyve, PI(3)P, PI(3,5)P2, and related molecules would be helpful. Response: To address this, we have added a schematic diagram illustrating the enzymatic relationships among PIKfyve, PI(3)P, PI(3,5)P₂, and related inositol phosphates. This schematic has been incorporated into the revised Fig. 2e to aid understanding of how UNI418 interacts with lipid kinase signaling pathways. Comment 6: • Fig. 3a: The authors report that RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP are downregulated upon UNI418 treatment. However, RAD51 remains at a detectable level. o I strongly recommend performing a quantitative proteomic analysis to determine how many proteins are affected by UNI418. Is RAD51 one of a few or one of many targets? Response: To address whether UNI418 broadly affects the proteome or selectively targets specific proteins, we conducted SILAC-based quantitative mass spectrometry in an independent validation experiment. The analysis indicated that UNI418 does not cause global protein degradation but instead affects a restricted subset of proteins. Notably, several replication-associated and chromatin-regulatory proteins, including MCM2, MCM5, MCM6, MCM7, and UHRF1, were consistently reduced upon UNI418 treatment. In contrast, RAD51 was not quantified in this dataset due to insufficient peptide coverage, likely reflecting low abundance and technical limitations of the LC–MS/MS run rather than lack of biological regulation. These results support our conclusion that UNI418 does not induce nonspecific proteolysis but instead modulates a defined set of proteins linked to DNA replication and genome stability. Because these SILAC data were performed as supportive validation and are not essential for the central conclusions of the manuscript, we did not include them in the revised figures. Nevertheless, we are happy to provide the data to the editor or reviewers upon request. Furthermore, we plan to reveal other proteins targeted by UNI418 using WDR5 interacting protein upon UNI418 treatment under proteasome inhibition. However, due to time limit for revision, constructing WDR5-BioID with inducible manner was not feasible. We plan to explore this direction in future. Comment 7: o The reduction in RAD51 should also be quantified from immunoblots and immunofluorescence (total levels, not just foci, if measurable). Response: As recommended, we performed quantitative analysis of RAD51 protein levels: - Western blot band intensities were quantified using ImageJ across ≥3 independent experiments. - RAD51 immunofluorescence (total nuclear signal, not only foci) was quantified using ZEN software. Both analyses consistently show a significant reduction in RAD51 upon UNI418 treatment. These quantifications have been added to the revised Fig. 3b and corresponding Extended Data Fig. 6b. Comment 8: o Please also consider the literature: heterozygosity of key HR genes (RAD51, BRCA1/2) often does not produce strong phenotypes. For example, comparisons to RAD51+/- versus -/- (or BRCA1+/- vs. BRCA1-/-) cells can be found elsewhere. Response: We have included additional discussion comparing our findings to known RAD51+/− and BRCA1+/− phenotypes. We believe that partial reduction rather than complete loss of RAD51 protein following UNI418 treatment causes mild but significant HR defect due to: - concurrent degradation of multiple HR regulators (RAD51, CHK1, CtIP), - UNI418 reduces RAD51 little more than half compared to RAD51+/-, - Cul4A activation amplifying proteolysis, - the requirement for precise stoichiometry in HR machinery. This explanation has been added in the Discussion to contextualize the observed phenotype. Comment 9: • Fig. 3b: A statistical analysis of UNI418 alone versus UNI418 + IR is warranted, as the remaining RAD51 foci formation appears different from the general BRCA1/2-deficient phenotype (no RAD51 foci formed). Response: As requested, we performed statistical analysis comparing the control, UNI418, IR, and UNI418 + IR conditions. Quantification of RAD51 foci in EdU-positive nuclei showed: - Control: ~6 foci - UNI418 alone: ~4 foci - IR (1 h): ~30 foci - UNI418 + IR (1 h): ~14 foci These analyses confirm that IR induces robust RAD51 foci formation, and that UNI418 reduces the number of IR-induced foci to an intermediate level. Statistical comparisons have been added to the revised figure, and the manuscript text has been updated accordingly. Comment 10: • Fig. 3c could be moved to Extended Data. Response: In accordance with this recommendation, Figure 3c has been moved to Extended Data Fig. 6c in the revised manuscript. Comment 11: • Fig. 3f: The reduction in HR frequency with UNI418 is much milder than with siRAD51. Please provide immunoblots of RAD51 under UNI418 and siRAD51 for comparison. Response: As requested, we have provided immunoblots comparing RAD51 protein levels under UNI418 treatment and siRAD51 knockdown, now included in Extended Data Fig. 7c. Consistent with the observed differences in HR frequency, siRAD51 almost completely depleted RAD51 protein, whereas UNI418 treatment resulted in a partial reduction, leaving a detectable residual level of RAD51. This difference in RAD51 depletion efficiency explains why the reduction in HR frequency by UNI418 appears milder than that observed with siRAD51. Comment 12: • Fig. 3g: “parp1-/-” should be capitalized as “PARP1-/-” since it refers to the human gene knockout. Response: Thanks for the comment. The notation has been corrected from parp1-/- to PARP1-/- throughout the manuscript, including in Figure 3g. Comment 13: • Fig. 3g and 3i: The authors used 0.25 µM UNI418, described as non-toxic to both cell types. If UNI418 is a catalytic inhibitor, why does its toxicity display clear dose dependence in PARP1-/- cells? Does RAD51 protein level also show dose-dependency by UNI418? o I am concerned that the apparent hypersensitivity of PARP1-/- cells by a dose-dependent UNI418 (1-5 uM >>0.25 uM) could reflect off-target effects, such as induction of PARP1-dependent DNA damage (base damage?). o Please include dose–response experiments (0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5 µM) to clarify this issue. Response: To address the concern, we performed dose–response analyses of UNI418 (0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5 µM) in both HCT116 WT and HCT116 PARP1-/- cells and examined RAD51, CHK1, CtIP, CUL4A, and γH2AX levels by immunoblotting (now included in Extended Data Fig. 8a). RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP showed a clear dose-dependent reduction in both WT and PARP1-/- cells. This pattern is consistent with our model in which UNI418 inhibits PIKfyve/PIP5K1C, decreases IP levels, and enhances Cul4A-mediated proteolysis of HR 6 factors. Importantly, the reduction is gradual rather than abrupt or irregular, which does not support an off-target toxicity effect. A dose-dependent increase in γH2AX was observed in PARP1-/- cells, and the magnitude was significantly higher than in WT cells. This heightened sensitivity is expected because PARP1-/- cells rely more heavily on HR to resolve replication-associated DNA damage; therefore, additional UNI418-mediated suppression of HR proteins leads to greater accumulation of DNA breaks. Together, these results support that the hypersensitivity of PARP1-/- cells reflects their increased dependence on HR rather than off-target toxicity of UNI418. Comment 14: • Fig. 4a: Since CHK1 is markedly reduced, its role in the drug sensitivity data must be considered. CHK1 inhibition is known to synergize with PARPi because PARPi-induced replication stress activates the ATR–CHK1 pathway. The authors should evaluate whether CHK1 suppression contributes to the observed olaparib sensitivity. Response: We agree with the reviewer that CHK1 plays a critical role in the cellular response to replication stress and that pharmacological or genetic suppression of CHK1 has been reported to synergize with PARP inhibition. PARPi-induced replication stress activates the ATR–CHK1 signaling axis, and inhibition of CHK1 compromises S-phase checkpoint control, leading to replication fork collapse and enhanced cytotoxicity. In our study, UNI418 treatment leads to a reduction in CHK1 protein levels concomitant with depletion of other HR-associated factors, including RAD51 and CtIP (Fig. 4a,b). We therefore acknowledge that CHK1 suppression is likely to contribute to the enhanced sensitivity to olaparib observed upon UNI418 treatment. However, several lines of evidence suggest that this effect cannot be attributed solely to CHK1 loss. First, UNI418 induces concurrent destabilization of multiple HR regulators rather than selectively targeting CHK1. Second, UNI418 markedly suppresses RAD51 foci formation and HR reporter activity, indicating a direct impairment of homologous recombination capacity. Third, the absence of additive effects between UNI418 treatment and genetic depletion of PIKfyve/PIP5K1C supports a shared upstream mechanism involving IP -dependent 6 Cul4A activation rather than isolated checkpoint inhibition. Taken together, our findings are consistent with a model in which UNI418-induced CHK1 reduction contributes to olaparib sensitivity as part of a broader HR-defective state, rather than acting as the sole driver of drug synergy. We have revised the Discussion to explicitly acknowledge the contribution of CHK1 suppression and to contextualize our results within the established ATR–CHK1–PARP interaction framework. Comment 15: • Fig. 4d: The sensitivity observed is mild (y-axis begins at 60%). HR-deficient cells are typically hypersensitive to olaparib at low micromolar or even nanomolar concentrations. o Please add control data for siBRCA1, siBRCA2, or siRAD51 cells for comparison. o The addition of UNI418 in these knockdown experiments (e.g., siPIKfyve + UNI418) would be informative. Response: To address this point, we performed additional experiments using siBRCA2 as HR- deficient control (Fig. 4d). As expected, BRCA2 knockdown increased sensitivity to olaparib, serving as a canonical HR-deficient reference. Notably, the extent of viability reduction observed upon dual depletion of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C was comparable to that seen with BRCA2 knockdown. We also examined whether UNI418 further enhances sensitivity when combined with siPIKfyve, siPIP5K1C, or the double knockdown (Fig. 4d). Interestingly, UNI418 treatment alone reduced viability to a similar extent, and additional knockdown of PIKfyve, PIP5K1C, or both did not further sensitize cells beyond the effect of UNI418 alone. These results suggest that the sensitizing effect of UNI418 and the combined depletion of PIKfyve/PIP5K1C converge on the same pathway, reflecting a shared mechanism involving decreased IP and consequent reduction of HR protein stability. 6 Comment 16: • Fig. 5a–b: The quantification is problematic. The Actin loading control is uneven, and the differences are marginal. Consider removing these panels if your conclusions remain supported without them. Response: In response to this concern—and consistent with similar comments from other reviewers—we repeated the experiments in Fig. 5a, including three independent biological replicates, and replaced the original panels with newly generated data. To verify that the upper CUL4A band represents the neddylated form, we additionally included MLN4924, a well-characterized neddylation inhibitor. As expected, MLN4924 treatment eliminated the upper band, confirming its identity as CUL4A–Nedd. Furthermore, we optimized sample loading and exposure conditions to ensure uniform Actin loading controls and clearer quantification across all replicates. The updated blots and quantification now show a consistent and reproducible reduction in CUL4A neddylation upon UNI418 treatment. Thus, with the improved data quality and proper validation using MLN4924, we believe these panels provide meaningful mechanistic support and have retained them in the revised manuscript. Comment 17: Please illustrate a pathway for how excess IP6 diminishes Cul4A neddylation Response: To address this point, we have revised the hypothetical model presented in Fig. 7j. Accordingly, we have added the following description to the figure legend of Fig. 7j: “Lipid kinases, such as PIKfyve and PIP5K1C, regulate cellular IP6 levels through the phosphatidylinositol signaling pathway. IP6 suppresses Cul4A ubiquitin ligase activity by promoting its deneddylation (N8) by the COP9 signalosome (CSN), thereby stabilizing key HR proteins such as RAD51 and CHK1.” Comment 18: • Fig. 5b: There is no additive effect of PIP5K1C knockdown and PIKfyve knockout, which appears inconsistent with Fig. 4d. Please discuss. Response: Although double depletion of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C results in a stronger reduction in cell viability compared to the single knockdowns (Fig. 4d), this additive effect is not reflected at the level of CUL4A neddylation (Fig. 5b). There are several biological reasons why these observations are not inconsistent. First, CUL4A neddylation appears to behave as a threshold- or saturation-type response. Our data indicate that knockdown of either PIKfyve or PIP5K1C alone is already sufficient to reduce IP6 to a level that maximally triggers CUL4A de-neddylation. As such, additional depletion of the second kinase may not further increase the magnitude of this biochemical readout. In contrast, cell viability represents a downstream, cumulative phenotype that integrates multiple layers of replication stress and impaired HR repair. Therefore, even if CUL4A de- neddylation does not further decrease beyond a threshold, the combined depletion of both kinases exacerbates cellular stress and leads to a more pronounced loss of viability. Taken together, the absence of an additive effect in CUL4A neddylation is consistent with a saturable mechanistic response upstream, whereas the stronger viability defect reflects downstream amplification of replication stress and HR deficiency. We have added this explanation to the revised manuscript. Comment 19: • Fig. 5c: RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP levels increase under siCUL4A, but also under UNI418 treatment. The authors should provide an unbiased interpretation. Response: We agree that the interpretation of Fig. 5c should be clearly described. siCUL4A alone increases RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP levels compared with control (C), consistent with the role of CUL4A as an E3 ligase promoting proteolysis of these proteins. UNI418 alone decreases RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP levels compared with control, in line with our model that UNI418 enhances Cul4A-dependent degradation of HR factors. When UNI418 and siCUL4A are combined, HR protein levels are elevated compared with UNI418 alone but do not fully return to the siCUL4A-only levels. We interpret this partial rescue as a consequence of incomplete depletion of CUL4A protein by siRNA treatment. Consistent with many E3 ligases, even modest residual amounts of CUL4A can retain biological activity. Thus, partial knockdown likely limits the extent to which CUL4A- dependent proteolysis can be fully suppressed, resulting in an incomplete recovery of HR protein levels under UNI418 treatment. Comment 20: • Fig. 6c: In siCtl cells, olaparib induces 20–40% cell death at 20–40 µM. Since the MOA of olaparib in HR-proficient cells is PARP trapping, these results need further explanation. How can siCUL4A or related treatments “rescue” HR-proficient cells? Excess RAD51 alone is unlikely to confer “super-HR” proficiency. Please consider alternative interpretations. Response: We note that olaparib can induce measurable cell death even in HR-proficient cells due to PARP1 trapping. The 20–40% decrease in viability in siCtrl cells at 20–40 µM olaparib is therefore consistent with the well-established cytotoxicity of PARP-trapping lesions in otherwise HR-competent cells. Importantly, the apparent “rescue” observed in siCUL4A cells should not be interpreted as enhanced HR capacity (“super-HR”). Instead, our data suggests an alternative explanation: CUL4A depletion partially alleviates replication-associated stress that is exacerbated by PARP trapping. Because CUL4A promotes proteolysis of several replication- and repair- associated proteins, its knockdown increases steady-state levels of multiple factors involved in maintaining replication fork stability. This general increase in replication- supporting proteins likely provides a modest buffering effect against PARP-trapping– induced stress, resulting in slightly improved survival relative to siCtrl. Thus, the reduced sensitivity to olaparib in siCUL4A cells does not reflect enhanced HR per se, but rather a broader dampening of replication stress via reduced CUL4A- mediated proteolysis. We have revised the manuscript to clarify this interpretation and avoid overstatement of HR dependence. Comment 21: • Fig. 7d, e, g, h: C4-2 and C2-2 cells (HR-proficient due to BRCA reversion mutations) are unexpectedly more sensitive to treatment. Please clarify why. Response: Although C4-2 and C2-2 cells restore BRCA2 function through reversion mutations and are categorized as HR-proficient, multiple studies have shown that BRCA-reverted cancer cells do not fully regain the genomic stability of genuinely HR-proficient cells. Instead, they retain elevated levels of replication stress and persistent genomic instability due to accumulated mutations and chromosomal rearrangements that arise prior to reversion. As a consequence, BRCA-reverted tumor cells remain highly dependent on robust HR and replication-stress response pathways for survival. Because UNI418 induces Cul4A-mediated degradation of essential HR factors—including RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP—the HR capacity of BRCA-reverted cells is disproportionately compromised upon UNI418 treatment. This heightened reliance on HR makes C4-2 and C2-2 cells more vulnerable to UNI418 compared with their parental BRCA2-deficient PEO-1 and Capan-1 cells. Consistent with this interpretation, UNI418 treatment led to a marked increase in apoptotic cell death specifically in C4-2 cells (Fig. 7i). This mechanistic vulnerability also explains why the combination of UNI418 and Olaparib produced stronger synthetic lethality in BRCA-reverted cells relative to parental lines. We have included this explanation in the revised manuscript. Comment 22: • As the authors noted in the Introduction, the synthetic lethality between PARP deficiency and BRCA1/2 deficiency is commonly explained by ssDNA gap accumulation, fork reversal, and transcription–replication collisions. To reproduce these effects, genuine HR deficiency together with PARP catalytic inhibition is required. Importantly, PARP catalytic inhibition is fully achieved at concentrations below 1 µM olaparib. However, the data shown in Figure 7 demonstrate a dose-dependent effect of olaparib in the range of 1–10 µM, which is unlikely to reflect catalytic inhibition but rather PARP trapping. This makes the apparent effectiveness of the UNI418 and PARP-/- combination difficult to interpret. Given that the precise mechanism of action of PARP inhibitors, particularly in BRCA-deficient backgrounds, remains controversial, the authors should avoid attributing their findings solely to PARP inhibition. Additional testing with DNA-damaging agents such as camptothecin or cisplatin would help to substantiate whether the observed effects indeed arise from HR defects. Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s detailed mechanistic insight. We agree that PARP catalytic inhibition is largely saturated at concentrations below 1 µM olaparib, and therefore the dose-dependent effects observed at 1–10 µM in Fig. 7 primarily reflect PARP–DNA trapping activity rather than catalytic inhibition alone. In the revised manuscript, we have clarified that the observed synthetic lethality between UNI418 and olaparib should not be interpreted exclusively through catalytic inhibition mechanisms. Importantly, our central conclusion—that UNI418 restores vulnerability in PARPi-resistant or BRCA-reverted cells by compromising HR capacity—does not rely solely on PARP inhibition. Multiple independent lines of evidence support HR impairment by UNI418: - UNI418 drives Cul4A-dependent degradation of RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP, leading to HR factor depletion (Fig. 3a; Extended Fig. 6). - RAD51 foci formation after IR is strongly suppressed by UNI418, particularly in S-phase cells (Fig. 3b). - HR reporter assays confirm significant loss of HR activity following UNI418 treatment (Fig. 3e). - UNI418 enhances γH2AX accumulation in PARP1–/– cells, consistent with increased DSB burden in HR-defective backgrounds (Extended Fig. 8a). In addition, to address the reviewer’s concern about whether UNI418-induced cellular responses extend beyond olaparib-specific contexts, we performed biochemical validation using alternative replication stress inducers. CPT or HU treatment revealed that CHK1, p-CHK1, and p-RPA32 levels decreased with ML367 and were further reduced with UNI418, while total RPA32 remained unchanged (Fig. 1d and e). These findings demonstrate that UNI418 suppresses replication stress signaling independent of PARP inhibitor exposure, further supporting our HR-defect model. Although we did not extend CPT or cisplatin experiments to full viability assays, we believe that the combined biochemical and functional data—spanning protein stability, RAD51 dynamics, foci formation, HR reporter output, and replication stress signaling—provide a strong mechanistic foundation for attributing UNI418 efficacy to HR pathway disruption rather than PARP-specific responses. Dear Editor and Reviewers, We have carefully addressed all remaining concerns and suggestions raised by the reviewers, and the manuscript has been revised accordingly. Detailed point-by-point responses are provided below. Reviewer #2 We sincerely thank you for your careful evaluation of our revised manuscript and for your constructive and supportive comments. We appreciate your recognition that the additional data and revisions have improved the study, and we are grateful for your specific suggestions to further strengthen clarity and presentation. We have now revised the manuscript accordingly and addressed all your remaining points. • Known abbreviations such as DSB are now defined at their first occurrence in the text. • The minor punctuation issue you noted (“by the FDA marks”) has been corrected. • Regarding your suggestion to briefly describe the target of Apilimod, we would like to note that this information was already stated earlier in the Results section (page 9, line 26 in the revised manuscript), where Apilimod is explicitly described as a PIKfyve inhibitor. • As suggested, we have added clarifying statements to the relevant figure legends indicating that the numbers shown above western blot bands represent quantified signal intensities normalized to the appropriate loading controls. • We have also included experimental confirmation of PARP1 loss in the HCT116 PARP1−/− cells, as requested (Extended Data Fig. 7d). All corresponding changes in the revised manuscript are marked in red text for clarity and ease of review. We thank you again for your helpful feedback, which has significantly improved the quality and clarity of our manuscript. Reviewer #4 We thank the reviewer for this important comment regarding the interpretation of Fig. 4d and the strength of olaparib sensitivity in BRCA2-depleted cells. We agree that the degree of sensitivity observed in the original CellTiter-Glo assay (72- hour treatment) appeared modest compared to the well-established hypersensitivity of bona fide BRCA2-deficient cells to PARP inhibitors. We note that the original experiment measured short-term metabolic viability after 3 days of drug exposure, which can underestimate long-term clonogenic cell death and primarily reflects proliferation and metabolic activity rather than sustained survival. To directly address this concern, we performed additional clonogenic survival assays using siBRCA2-treated cells under prolonged olaparib exposure (7-day growth). Under these conditions, BRCA2 knockdown cells showed strong hypersensitivity to olaparib, with more than 50% reduction in colony formation even at low olaparib concentrations, consistent with canonical HR-deficient responses to PARP inhibition. Importantly, when we performed the same clonogenic assay for siPIKfyve, siPIP5K1C, and double knockdown conditions, the overall response pattern was consistent with the CellTiter-Glo results, supporting the relative interpretation presented in Fig. 4d. These new clonogenic data are now provided in Extended Data Fig. 8d. We have revised the manuscript to clarify the differences between the CellTiter-Glo viability assay and the clonogenic survival assay and to note that the clonogenic data confirm robust Olaparib hypersensitivity in BRCA2-depleted cells.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors made a complete revision of the manuscript They answer to all my point
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: In the revised version of the manuscript by Lee et al., the authors thoroughly addressed most of my concerns. With inclusion new data and revisions, I agree that carrying out a cell cycle resolved time course to monitor foci of different DSBs falls outside the scope of the study. We appreciate the authors stating they will address investigating re-sensitization of other mechanisms of PARPi-resistance in a future study. We have caught a few minor text edits and suggestions that ideally should be addressed to ensure the final version of the study is the best it can be. 1. There are a few undefined abbreviations in the text: for example, “DSB” needs to be defined at its first instance of used, page 4 on line 11. 2. “… by the FDA, marks …” Line 20, remove the comma between FDA and marks. 3. On page 9, line 32, we suggest the author includes a brief description of the target(s) of Apilimod to help better inform and orient the reader to the authors main points. 4. We appreciate the author including the quantification of western blot signal in the relevant figures. As a point of clarity for the reader, we suggest they include in the figure caption of the relevant figures that the numbers above the band represent signal quantification of the band in reference to the appropriate loading control. 5. Regarding the HCT116 PARP1-/- cells used in this study, we would appreciate if the authors included a western blot or used another method to confirm the loss of the PARP1 protein in this cell line.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: I appreciate the authors’ efforts to address the reviewers’ comments and to include additional experiments in the revised manuscript. However, I remain concerned about the interpretation of Fig. 4d, which I believe requires further consideration. In Fig. 4d, siBRCA2 is presented as a canonical HR-deficient positive control for olaparib sensitivity. However, under the current experimental conditions, BRCA2 knockdown results in only ~20% reduction in viability even at 10 µM olaparib. This degree of sensitivity is unexpectedly mild for HR-deficient cells and does not align with the well-established hypersensitivity of bona fide BRCA2-deficient cells to PARP inhibitors, which typically manifests at low micromolar or even sub-micromolar concentrations. This raises the question of whether bona fide cell death is occurring under these conditions, or whether the observed effect instead reflects a modest slowing of cell-cycle progression or proliferation. In this context, it is difficult to interpret the data as measuring the canonical cytotoxic effect of olaparib in HR-deficient cells. Given this limited response, it is difficult to consider the siBRCA2 condition in Fig. 4d as a robust or appropriate positive control for HR deficiency. As a consequence, the conclusion that dual depletion of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C produces an effect “comparable to BRCA2 knockdown” is not fully convincing.I therefore strongly encourage the authors to further optimize or reconsider the experimental conditions used in Fig. 4d (e.g., efficiency of BRCA2 depletion, drug concentration range, assay sensitivity, or choice of HR-proficient cells).
