Below, we provide a detailed, point-by-point response, and all changes have been incorporated into the revised manuscript. We believe these revisions have significantly improved the clarity and impact of our work. Reviewer #1 Comment 1: Fig1c The error bars for the measurements with no 5-FUrd are missing Response: The error bars for the “no 5-FUrd” condition are included; however, the variation in these measurements is extremely small, and therefore the error bars are not visually discernible at the current graph scale. To ensure transparency, we have provided the exact numerical values for each data point in the Source Data file. Comment 2: In Fig1d we cannot see the effect of ML367 on RPA32 phosphorylation at 0.5µM. The authors may present the same figures with both inhibitors at 2.5µM where ML367 has an effect. Ext Data Fig1d. Interestingly, UNI418 treatment reduced the level of CHK1 as well as its phosphorylation, even in the absence of DNA replication stress” It is not obvious that in presence of UNI418 and in absence of 5-FUrd. The level of Chk1 is reduced but not its phosphorylated form. Ext Data Fig1d: The experiment in presence of ML367 is not reported. CHK1 expression level in presence of UNI418 “Interestingly, UNI418 treatment reduced the level of CHK1 as well as its phosphorylation, even in the absence of DNA replication stress, suggesting it affects CHK1 expression.” The authors may comment on why they have not analyzed the CHK1 mRNA level to further assert this statement. Response: As several reviewers raised similar concerns, we performed additional experiments to clarify the effects of UNI418 and ML367 on CHK1 and phosphor-CHK1 levels. For these new experiments, we adjusted the concentration of ML367 to 10 µM, at which its effects were more clearly detectable than at 0.5 µM. Our new data show that, even in the absence of 5-FUrd, UNI418 reduces both p-CHK1 and total CHK1 levels more robustly than ML367. We also observed the same trend under 5-FUrd treatment, indicating that UNI418 consistently suppresses CHK1 signaling regardless of replication stress conditions (now Extended Data Fig. 1b). Furthermore, as presented in Extended Data Fig. 6e, UNI418 does not alter CHK1 mRNA levels under replication-stress-free conditions, suggesting that the reduction in CHK1 protein is not driven by transcriptional downregulation. We have updated the figures and the corresponding text to reflect these new findings. Comment 3: PIP5KIC samples. The calculated dissociation constant (KD) of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C was 0.78 nM, and 61 nM, respectively. The reviewer did not find the protocol used to express and purify PIP5KIC or provider’s name. Response: Thanks for the comment. We have now added the relevant details to the Methods section of the manuscript. Specifically, we have included the following description: “The gene encoding the kinase domain of human PIKfyve and PIP5K1C was amplified from GFP-hPIKfyve and GFP-PIPK1 gamma 90 (GFP-PIP5K1C) plasmids purchased from Addgene (#121148 and #22299), and cloned into the expression vector pVFT4S, which contains a poly-histidine tag, a maltose-binding protein (MBP), and a tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease recognition site.” This added information clarifies the source of the constructs and the cloning strategy used for protein expression and purification. Comment 4: Quality of protein samples used. The authors should put in ED an SDS-PAGE of the purified proteins Response: Thanks for the comment. To address the concern regarding the quality of the purified proteins samples, we have now included an SDS-PAGE gel image in Extended Data Fig. 3a, which shows the purity of the proteins used in this study. Comment 5: Fig2 KD (nM) values of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C inhibition were determined using the SelectScreen kinase assay. The authors should briefly explain in the M&M or in ED the principle of this assay. There are no Y axis or X-axis labels in Fig2D! There are no error bars, and the quality should be improved. Response: We have added a brief explanation of the SelectScreen® kinase assay to the Methods section of the revised manuscript, describing the assay principle and workflow used to determine KD values for PIKfyve and PIP5K1C. Specifically, the following description has been included in the Methods section: “Kinase assays were performed using the SelectScreen® Kinase Profiling platform (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Kinase-tagged T7 phages were produced in an E. coli BL21- derived host, and additional kinases were expressed in HEK293 cells and subsequently DNA-tagged for qPCR detection. Streptavidin-coated magnetic beads were incubated with biotinylated small-molecule ligands to generate affinity resins, followed by blocking with buffer to minimize nonspecific binding. Binding reactions were assembled by mixing kinases, ligand-coupled beads, and test compounds in binding buffer (20% SeaBlock, 0.17× PBS, 0.05% Tween-20, 6 mM DTT). Test compounds were applied as an 11-point 3-fold serial dilution series, with a final DMSO concentration of 0.9%. Reactions were carried out in 384-well plates at a final volume of 20 µL and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. Beads were then washed and resuspended in elution buffer containing 0.5 µM non-biotinylated ligand. The concentration of eluted kinases was quantified by qPCR, and dissociation constants (KD) were determined from concentration–response curves.” Sorry not to provide better graph in the original submission. We have improved the quality of Fig 2d (now Fig. 2b) by replacing the original graph which was provided by the company with a newly generated version using GraphPad Prism with actual dataset, which now includes clear X- and Y-axis labels, error ranges and higher graphical clarity. Comment 6: SPR analyses the blank-subtracted sensorgram data unequivocally demonstrated the direct interaction of UNI418 Precise what is the blank substracted? without UNI418 but on chip with or without MBP? ED Fig4 There was no interaction between UNI418 and MBP, which was fused to the kinases used in this study for purification (Extended Data Fig. 4). The signals with only MBP at 10µM are about 5RU vs 12RU for UNI418 substracted with (MBP or buffer?). The difference is not sufficient to say, “no interaction”. Rephrase. The fits are poor. Comment. The number after comma is meaningless. The experiment should be done in triplicate so that the KD errors are not the errors of one fit but of triplicate experiments Response: In our SPR experiments, the term “blank” refers to the signal obtained when the chip is immobilized with MBP–PIKfyve or MBP–PIP5K1C and an injection containing only DMSO— at the same concentration used to solubilize UNI418—is flowed over the surface. This subtraction step removes refractive-index changes and bulk shifts originating from DMSO, ensuring that the sensorgrams reflect only the binding response induced by UNI418 itself. This clarification has been added to the revised manuscript. “UNI418 was then injected as an analyte over the chip surface, and changes in resonance units (RU), which reflect molecular mass accumulation on the sensor surface, were monitored. Sensorgrams were generated to visualize the interaction kinetics. To ensure accurate measurement of compound-specific binding, sensorgrams were blank- subtracted using signals obtained from injections containing DMSO alone at the same concentration used to solubilize UNI418.” In Extended Data Fig. 4 (now Extended Data Fig 3b), we immobilized purified MBP alone on the chip and injected UNI418 at 1, 2, 5, and 10 µM. Although MBP produced a small RU response, the signal decreased over time, indicating that the interaction is transient and unlikely to represent a specific binding event. These data were included to demonstrate that the responses observed when MBP–PIKfyve or MBP–PIP5K1C were immobilized are not attributable to nonspecific interaction with the MBP tag but instead arise from specific interaction with the respective kinase domains. Regarding the fitting quality, UNI418 requires DMSO for solubility. The experiment was performed using the highest DMSO concentration recommended for Biacore instruments, which inevitably limits curve-fitting quality. While slight deviations are observed at higher analyte concentrations, the predicted fit curves follow the experimental data reasonably well across the full concentration range. Importantly, we performed the experiment in three independent replicates, and the calculated KD values were highly consistent across repeats, supporting the robustness of the measurements. The replicate sensorgrams and KD calculations are provided in the Source Data file, and the KD values reported in the revised manuscript now include error estimates derived from these triplicate experiments. Comment 7: CETSA assay. The CETSA assays are useful and convincing experiments. What is a made in triplicate? If so, please add in sources file. Response: We confirm that the CETSA assays were performed in three independent biological replicates. The full raw data from all three replicates are included in the Source Data file, as requested. Comment 8: PIPK roles in membrane trafficking “Lipid kinases, including PIKfyve and PIP5K1C, play crucial roles in phosphorylating inositol-containing molecules, which are integral to various cellular signaling pathways as second messengers.” The authors should mention that PIPK are also involved in membrane trafficking. It is only mentioned in the Discussion section. Response: The sentence “Lipid kinases, including PIKfyve and PIP5K1C, play crucial roles in phosphorylating inositol-containing molecules, which are integral to various cellular signaling pathways as second messengers.” appears in the Results section of the original manuscript and introduces the enzymatic and signaling characteristics of these kinases. In addition, we agree with the reviewer that PIKfyve and PIP5K1C also play important roles in membrane trafficking. To address this point, we have further emphasized their trafficking-related functions in the Discussion section. Specifically, we added the following text: “The tumor regression induced by UNI418 may rely not only on HR protein degradation but also on pleiotropic effects associated with PIKfyve and PIP5K1C inhibition. These lipid kinases regulate the generation of PI(3,5)P and PI(4,5)P , which are essential for 2 2 endosomal and lysosomal membrane dynamics as well as autophagy activation. Therefore, UNI418-mediated disruption of cellular homeostasis may contribute to the observed antitumor response.” Comment 9: Chemical schema of inositol species. The authors should add in the ED the scheme of all inositol species mentioned in the manuscript for less specialist readers. Response: Thanks for the suggestion. We have added a schematic representation of all inositol species mentioned in the manuscript to Fig. 2e, so that readers who are less familiar with inositol metabolism can more easily follow the content. This addition has been incorporated into the revised manuscript. Comment 10: ED Fig 5C. The authors should improve the ED Fig5c so that the reader may better evaluate the reduction of IP6. Response: To more clearly demonstrate the reduction of IP6 levels upon UNI418 treatment, we performed the experiment again with three independent replicates. The data were re- plotted using Prism to improve clarity and readability, and the updated graph has been incorporated into now Extended Data Fig. 4c in the revised manuscript. Comment 11: ED with 3D modelling of UNI418 position. The authors should add in ED a zoom view of the superimposition of the ATP with UNI418 from the Rosetta dock prediction with surrounding residues. Response: Following the recommendation, we have added a zoomed-in view showing the superimposition of ATP and UNI418 from the Rosetta docking prediction, along with the surrounding residues. The authors should give error bars based on triplicate. Three decimals precision is surprising. Correct. Comment 14: Rephrase UNI418-mediated reduction in HR frequency, attributed to the proteolysis of HR proteins by activated Cul4A ubiquitin ligase following down-regulation of IP via 6 inhibition of PIKfyve/PIP5K1C by UNI418, was also restored upon additional supplementation of IP Rephrase! Suggestion. “UNI418-mediated reduction in HR 6 frequency was also restored upon additional supplementation of IP . 6 Response: As recommended, we have revised the sentence to the clearer phrasing: “UNI418-mediated reduction in HR frequency was also restored upon additional supplementation of IP .” This change has been incorporated into the revised manuscript. 6 Comment 15: IP6 toxicity However, it is important to note that IP exhibited toxicity in both WT and 6 parp1-/- cells. The authors may show in ED the data. Response: In our study, IP supplementation was performed as a brief 10-minute treatment. Comment 16: Partial knockdown In contrast, WDR5 knockdown did not increase CtIP levels (data not shown). The authors mention here and elsewhere “knockdown” of proteins while the levels of the proteins upon siRNA treatments are only weakened. They should precise and comment the potential impact of residual levels of the proteins. Response: As described in the manuscript, our screening strategy was designed to identify the DCAF responsible for RAD51 proteolysis. Based on the established role of DCAFs in determining Cul4A substrate specificity, we screened more than 60 predicted DCAFs using siRNAs and monitored RAD51 and CHK1 levels. WDR5 was the only candidate whose silencing consistently increased both proteins, and we therefore focused our analysis on WDR5 as the relevant DCAF. WDR5 was identified through screening with RAD51 and CHK1 as readouts. However, WDR5 knockdown shows minimal or no effect on CtIP, which is likely regulated by a different DCAF or degradation pathway. We commented it in the revised manuscript. Furthermore, to assess whether residual protein levels from partial knockdown may influence the results, we performed experiments under MG132 treatment, which fully blocks proteolysis. Under these conditions, the effects of WDR5 and CUL4A knockdown were further enhanced, supporting the conclusion that the observed phenotypes were indeed limited by the presence of residual protein. We commented it in the revised manuscript. “In contrast, WDR5 knockdown did not increase CtIP levels (data not shown), which suggest CtIP is regulated by other DCAF. Additional proteasome inhibition using MG132 showed further enhancement of the observed effects, suggesting that residual protein levels due to incomplete knockdown of WDR5 and CUL4A may have masked the full recovery of RAD51 and CHK1 (data not shown).” This figure is not included in the revised manuscript. It is only for reviewers. Comment 17: Fig. 6d, the authors should add the level of RFWD3 in presence of siRNA. Response: To examine RFWD3 levels upon siRNA treatment, we purchased the commercially available antibody cited in previously published studies and performed immunoblotting. However, the antibody did not yield a detectable or specific signal under our experimental conditions, making it difficult to reliably assess RFWD3 protein levels. As an alternative, we measured RFWD3 mRNA expression by qPCR, and these results were added to Extended Data Fig. 9g in the revised manuscript. Comment 18: Combined use of UNI418 and Oliparib Crucially, this increase in drug sensitivity was paralleled by a marked elevation in apoptotic cell death among the PARPi resistant C4-2 cells following UNI418 treatment The effect is less significative with combined use of UNI418 and Oliparib. The authors may indicate and comment. Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue. Upon careful re-examination of the data used in the original submission, we identified an error in the dataset associated with the apoptotic cell death analysis in the combination treatment condition. This error affected the apparent magnitude of the effect observed with the combined use of UNI418 and Olaparib. We have now corrected the dataset, re-plotted the graphs, and re-performed the statistical analyses using the corrected values. Following this correction, the revised data accurately reflect the effects of UNI418 alone and in combination with Olaparib in PARPi- resistant C4-2 cells. The updated figures and statistical analyses have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Fig. 7i). We apologize for any confusion caused by the initial error and appreciate the reviewer’s careful assessment, which helped us improve the accuracy and clarity of the presented data. Comment 19: Redundancy End of results part and beginning of discussion are redundant. Response: We agree that the opening statement of the Discussion section partially overlapped with the concluding paragraph of the Results. To address this redundancy, we have removed the overlapping explanatory sentences from the beginning of the Discussion and reorganized the opening paragraph to ensure that the Discussion section no longer repeats information presented in the Results. Reviewer #2 Comment 1: Data transparency – To facilitate data transparency, I suggest the authors show individual data points on all graphs so that readers get a better sense of the data distribution in experiments. Response: In accordance with the recommendation, we have revised all graphs throughout the manuscript to display individual data points. These updated figures are included in the revised manuscript. Comment 2: Western blot quantification – The authors mention several times that protein levels are significantly or substantially changed between different treatment conditions, but do not consistently present quantified data of relevant immunoblots supported with statistical tests to back up these otherwise only qualitative claims. I recommend that the authors include relevant quantifications of immunoblot data (where these claims are directed) to better support any assertions. The use of superlatives to describe changes should also be limited and/or fully removed, as these have limited quantitative meaning. Response: To address this concern, we have now included quantitative analyses for the key immunoblot data supporting our conclusions. For the relevant experiments, three independent biological replicates were performed, and representative full immunoblot images from all repeats have been provided in the Source Data files. Band intensities were quantified using ImageJ, and values were normalized to the appropriate loading controls (α-tubulin, GAPDH, or histone H3, as indicated for each experiment). The normalized values are now displayed numerically above each corresponding band in the figures. Comment 3: DNA Replication Stress Response – In figure 1, the authors measure DNA replication stress response suppression by induction of ATAD5. I am wondering how inhibition by the two small molecule inhibitors compares to inhibition of CHK1 phosphorylation via ATR inhibition, as that could be a good positive control for suppression of certain facets of the DNA replication stress response. Response: To address this point, we incorporated ATR inhibitor (ATRi) as a positive control for suppression of the DNA replication stress response. In the revised figure, we now directly compare each treatment condition individually—ML367, UNI418, and ATRi—by examining their respective effects on p-CHK1 and total CHK1 levels. Comment 4: DNA replication stress response inhibition – Induction of ATAD5 between ML367 and UNI418 are different in figure 1C, making it difficult to make any comparison about suppression of DNA replication stress response as currently presented in the manuscript. Another interpretation could be that both inhibitors function similarly as they both result in ~75% reduction in signals at the highest concentration of inhibitors. Furthermore, the authors do not make any comparisons between dissociation constants or IC between 50 ML367 and UNI418 in the text, which would allow readers to draw conclusions about whether UNI418 displays heightened suppression of the DNA replication stress response. I suggest the authors make mention of these values to support their claims. Response: Thanks for the comment. To clarify the relative effects of ML367 and UNI418 on the DNA replication stress response, we examined the quantitative values provided in the Source Data for ATAD5 luciferase activity. At the highest concentration tested (5 µM), ML367 reduced ATAD5 luciferase activity by approximately 70% compared to the 5-FUrd–treated control, whereas UNI418 reduced the signal by approximately 90% under the same conditions. These measurements indicate a substantially stronger suppression of replication stress signaling by UNI418 relative to ML367. To facilitate interpretation of these differences, we have updated Fig. 1c to report the IC values for ATAD5 luciferase activity, which further substantiates the conclusion that 50 UNI418 more potently suppresses the replication stress response. Comment 5: RAD51 Foci quantification in Figure 3 – please describe if this was done manually or whether an automated foci detection system was used. If the latter was used, please provide a brief description of the pipeline in the methods section. a. It is also important to understand whether cells in G2 phase were distinguished from cells in S-phase (at the time of irradiation / analysis of foci), as DSB repair processes between each phase are distinct. In the context of this work, selective analysis of cells irradiated in S-phase and analyzed in S-phase would be most logical. b. The legends indicate that these cells were monitored 1 hour after 10 Gy, a dose and time point that I am honestly very surprised that “only” an average of ~15 RAD51 foci are observed in the control / DMSO. From experience and understanding of comparable literature, foci numbers at least twice this are anticipated, as 10 Gy would be predicted to induce 100-200 DNA breaks in a G1 phase cell and 200-400 breaks in a G2 phase cell (with intermediate numbers in S-phase) depending on cell type genome content. While not all IR-induced breaks will undergo HR and form RAD51, at least 1/3 of induced breaks at any given time are expected to. It is not uncommon for radiation dosimetry here to vary substantially between groups if irradiator calibration is not up-to-date, or it could be possible that too many breaks are occurring and challenging for the authors to separate (foci are merging). I would advise the authors to examine this issue more closely in the context of what is understood from the published literature, as these numbers do appear far less than expected for that dose. c. Finally, while Figure 3b is helpful, it is a single time point and understanding whether the UNI418 specific effect is transient by performing a few timepoints in addition to the 1h would be helpful. Response: Thanks for the comment. RAD51 foci were quantified using confocal microscopy followed by semi-automated analysis in ZEN software (Carl Zeiss). Images were acquired on an LSM880 confocal microscope using identical acquisition settings for all samples. After background subtraction, nuclei were segmented based on DAPI, and RAD51 foci were quantified exclusively in EdU-positive nuclei, which had been identified following Click-iT detection. Foci were detected using the ZEN spot detection module with fixed thresholding parameters applied uniformly across all samples. Quantification was performed on ≥50 EdU-positive nuclei per condition. These details have been added to the Methods section. To address reviewer’s comment, we redid experiments several times more after recalibrating our x-ray machine. a. To address concerns regarding cell-cycle heterogeneity, we restricted our analysis to S-phase cells identified by EdU incorporation. Cells were pulse-labeled with EdU after irradiation, followed by Click-iT detection immediately prior to imaging. Only EdU-positive nuclei were included in the RAD51 foci quantification. This clarification has been added to Fig. 3b. b. b. In our repeated experiments, S-phase cells exhibited an average of more than 30 RAD51 foci at the 1 h time point. Reported values in the literature vary substantially depending on cell type, irradiation conditions, and quantification methods, ranging widely from ~20 to >80 foci. Therefore, the values observed in our experiments fall within the variability reported across published studies. c. In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we examined RAD51 foci at 1 h, 3 h, and 6 h after irradiation. The suppressive effect of UNI418 on RAD51 foci was observed at all timepoints, indicating that the effect is not transient. Comment 6: DSB Repair Efficiency – In figure 3F, the authors show both a large reduction in HR efficiency and a small reduction in NHEJ efficiency when cells are treated with UNI418 in the I-Sce1 plasmid reporter assay. Testing whether the repair of genomic breaks by monitoring foci numbers in G1, S, and G2 cells over a time course following some other form of genotoxic stress would further support the claims of reduced repair efficiency and validate the observations with the plasmid-based assay, which are otherwise not able to distinguish effects between phases. HU, IR, ATR inhibitors, Camptothecin, or even endogenous DNA replication stress might be used in this context – with the most important thing being to monitor damage formed and resolved in S-phase separately from other phases. Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion. We fully agree that monitoring DSB repair kinetics in G1, S, and G2 cells following genotoxic stress would provide additional mechanistic insight. However, performing a full cell-cycle–resolved time-course analysis using multiple markers (γH2AX, 53BP1, RAD51) is beyond the scope and technical feasibility of the current revision timeline. Importantly, our study already incorporates several complementary assays that directly assess HR repair efficiency in S-phase cells: • EdU-based RAD51 foci quantification (Fig. 3b), • I-SceI DR-GFP reporter assay (Fig. 3e), • Effects of UNI418 on replication-stress–induced DDR signaling (Fig. 1), all of which consistently demonstrate that UNI418 markedly reduces HR activity. While we agree that additional time-course experiments could provide further detail, the combined results from our existing assays robustly support the conclusion that UNI418 impairs HR-mediated DSB repair. Comment 7: Synthetic lethality with Olaparib – it would be interesting to see how cell survival in the combination treatment compares to cell survival when BRCA1 or BRCA2 are knocked down by siRNA, as this is the canonical example of synthetic lethality in DNA repair. Response: To address this point, we performed additional experiments using siBRCA2 as HR- deficient control (Fig. 4d). As expected, BRCA2 knockdown increased sensitivity to olaparib, serving as a canonical HR-deficient reference. Notably, the extent of viability reduction observed upon dual depletion of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C was comparable to that seen with BRCA2 knockdown. Comment 8: PARPi resistance and re-sensitization – In Figure 7, the authors examine PARPi resistance by BRCA2 reversion, but there are quite a few known and different mechanisms that cells (especially cancer cells) can leverage to become more resistant to PARPi action. It would be interesting to see whether BRCA1/2 negative cells that have restored homologous recombination repair due to TP53BP1 loss, or resistance due to increased efflux pump expression, are re-sensitized to PARPi when treated with UNI418. Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion. We fully agree that PARP inhibitor resistance can arise through multiple mechanisms, including TP53BP1 loss–mediated restoration of HR and drug efflux pump upregulation. Testing whether UNI418 re- sensitizes such models would indeed provide additional mechanistic insight. However, generating or obtaining TP53BP1-deficient BRCA1/2 mutant lines or efflux pump–overexpressing PARPi-resistant models, and validating their resistance mechanisms, is beyond the scope and technical feasibility of the current revision timeline. We will evaluate whether UNI418 could restore PARPi sensitivity to other types of resistant mechanisms in future study. Importantly, our study already demonstrates that UNI418 re-sensitizes PARPi-resistant cells driven by BRCA2 reversion, a clinically relevant resistance mechanism. Together with the consistent HR suppression shown in multiple independent assays (RAD51 foci, DR-GFP reporter, DDR signaling), our results strongly support the conclusion that UNI418 enhances PARPi sensitivity by targeting HR restoration. Comment 9: Big Picture – It is not clear within the discussion whether the authors think that their tool compounds can be modified for therapeutic purposes, and this would be helpful. I was also expecting some discussion about differences in IP and related biosynthetic 6 processes between normal and cancer cells, and between different cancer types that naturally would have plenty of metabolic variation given their context and specific genomic profile. Response: To address these points, we expanded the Discussion to incorporate broader therapeutic implications of UNI418 and to introduce biological differences in IP metabolism relevant 6 to cancer contexts. Specifically, we added a paragraph that discusses cancer-type– associated variation in IP biosynthetic enzymes and their potential influence on tumor 6 biology and treatment vulnerability: “In addition to these mechanistic findings, accumulating evidence suggests that IP6 metabolism itself may differ across cancer types. While UNI418 does not directly target IP6K or IPMK, dysregulation of these upstream enzymes has been associated with tumor biology and clinical prognosis. IP6K2 functions as a tumor suppressor in breast cancer, whereas IP6K1 upregulation correlates with aggressive recurrence and poor survival outcomes. These data suggest that distinct nodes within the inositol phosphate network are differentially exploited by malignancies. Tumors heavily dependent on HR and IP6 metabolic wiring may therefore be uniquely vulnerable to agents—such as UNI418—that reduce cellular IP pools. Future comparative metabolomic and genomic analyses across 6 tumor lineages will be essential for defining biomarkers that predict UNI418 sensitivity and guide clinical application. Taken together, these findings establish a mechanistic link between inositol phosphate signaling, HR dependency, and exploitable therapeutic vulnerabilities in DNA repair–dependent cancers, including those with BRCA dysfunction or PARPi resistance.” Comment 10: “DNA repair” – throughout this manuscript, the words “DNA repair” are used to actually refer to “DNA double strand break repair” or similar. The processes being discussed here are specific to that type of DNA damage in the context of DNA replication, and not all possible types of DNA damage that exist. Please amend all instances of that language to be specific. Response: Thanks for thoughtful comments. We fully agree that the term “DNA repair” was at times used in a broad manner, whereas the processes discussed in our study relate specifically to DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair mechanisms, particularly those occurring during DNA replication. To address this, we carefully revised the manuscript to ensure that terminology is used with appropriate specificity throughout. In all relevant sections—Introduction, Results, and Discussion—we replaced general references to “DNA repair” with more accurate terms such as “DNA double-strand break repair,” “DSB repair,” or “HR-dependent DSB repair,” depending on the context. Comment 11: Western blot loading control –In figure 1b, the appropriate loading control for pRPA32 is total RPA32 levels, please include this control. H3 is less ideal in the context of that experiment. Response: We agree that total RPA32 serves as a more appropriate loading control for pRPA32 analysis. To address the reviewer’s request, we additionally treated cells with CPT and HU and examined CHK1, p-CHK1, p-RPA32, and total RPA32 levels. The results indicate that CHK1, p-CHK1, and p-RPA32 were reduced in ML367-treated cells and further decreased upon UNI418 treatment, whereas total RPA32 levels remained unchanged (Fig 1d, 1e). In Extended Fig. 1b, we showed that 5-FUrd treatment decreased p- CHK1 and CHK1 in ML367-treated cells and further reduced p-CHK1 and CHK1 in UNI418-treated cells. Comment 12: How these inhibitors are referred to – generally it is advisable to be specific and call them PARP1/2-trapping inhibitors, as other small molecules that block PARP enzyme action exist, with no to variable impact on trapping PARP enzymes at sites of DNA leading to damage. Response: We agree that the term “PARP inhibitors” can be ambiguous, as it encompasses both catalytic inhibitors and clinically used agents that induce PARP1/2 trapping. To address this, the sentence in the Introduction has been updated to: “The approval of clinically used PARP1/2-trapping inhibitors (commonly referred to as PARP inhibitors, PARPis), such as Olaparib, Niraparib, Rucaparib, Veliparib, and Talazoparib, by the US FDA, marks a pivotal advancement in the treatment of breast and ovarian cancers carrying BRCA mutations.” We have applied this terminology consistently throughout the revised manuscript. Comment 13: Data normalization –In Figure 1a, it is not clearly stated whether the Luc-ATAD5 data is normalized or not. The authors should revise all figures and clearly state whether the data is normalized, and if so, what the data is normalized to. Response: In Figure 1a, the Luc-ATAD5 activity was normalized to the NT (non-treated) control, which was set to 1, and all other values are presented as relative fold changes. We have now clarified this in the figure legend. We also carefully reviewed other figures and added explicit descriptions of normalization methods in the corresponding legends wherever necessary to ensure consistency and transparency in data presentation. Comment 14: Phosphorylation of CHK1 – I would suggest including the blot of phospho-CHK1 in the main body of the manuscript in figure 1. Comment 15: Kinase screen – I suggest the authors include extended data figure 2 in the main body as it guides the narrative of the study. I would also ask for more details on what precent control is referring to, and that the authors label the kinases of interest within the plot to make it more clear to the reader. Given this limited response, it is difficult to consider the siBRCA2 condition in Fig. 4d as a robust or appropriate positive control for HR deficiency. As a consequence, the conclusion that dual depletion of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C produces an effect “comparable to BRCA2 knockdown” is not fully convincing.I therefore strongly encourage the authors to further optimize or reconsider the experimental conditions used in Fig. 4d (e.g., efficiency of BRCA2 depletion, drug concentration range, assay sensitivity, or choice of HR-proficient cells).

## Paper

## Abstract

Homologous recombination (HR) is crucial for maintaining genomic integrity and is tightly
regulated, yet the role of ubiquitin-dependent degradation in HR proteins remains poorly
understood. Through high-throughput screening for compounds that modulate the DNA

suppresses HR, enhances tumor sensitivity to PARP inhibitors (PARPis), and re-

## Introduction

Genomic instability is a hallmark characteristic of most cancer cells, which is supported
by mounting evidence indicating that impaired DNA repair fosters mutator phenotypes
and chromosomal abnormalities, thereby accelerating cellular transformation 1, 2.
Homologous recombination (HR) is a high-fidelity DNA repair pathway that resolves DSBs
using a homologous DNA template. This process is essential for maintaining genome
stability, particularly during the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle when a sister chromatid
is available 3. RAD51, which is a major recombinase in HR, functions by forming
nucleoprotein filaments on single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and facilitating strand invasion
into homologous sequences, enabling error-free double-strand break (DSB) repair. Given
its essential role in genome integrity, RAD51 exprRession is tightly regulated at multiple
levels, including transcription, post-transcriptional modifications, and post-translational
mechanisms. RAD51 expression is regulateNd by various transcription factors in response
to DNA damage and cell cycle progression. The tumor suppressor p53 represses RAD51
transcription under genotoxic stress, preventing excessive HR that could lead to genomic
instability 4. E2F1 positively regCulates RAD51 expression, particularly during the S and
G2 phases of the cell cycle, when HR is most active 5. Compared to the well-established
understanding of RADR51 mRNA regulation, the regulation of RAD51 protein levels
remains relatively unexplored. The E3 ubiquitin ligase RFWD3 has been identified as a
ubiquitin ligase that affects both the single-stranded DNA-binding protein RPA and RAD51
on chromatin 6.

Cullin 4A (Cul4A) is a scaffold protein in the CRL4 ubiquitin ligase complex 7, which
includes Damage-Specific DNA Binding Protein 1 (DDB1) and DDB1-CUL4 Associated
Factors (DCAFs). Cul4A plays a crucial role in maintaining genome stability by targeting
key regulatory proteins for ubiquitin-mediated degradation. Dysregulation of Cul4A has
been implicated in various cancers, promoting cell proliferation, genomic instability, and
therapy resistance.

The increased genomic instability observed in cancer frequently originates from
deficiencies in one or more DNA repair pathways, often providing cancer cells with a
selective advantage in advancing toward a more malignant phenotype. These defects
compel cancer cells to rely on the remaining functional DNA repair mechanisms for
survival, particularly considering the heightened proliferation rates 8. Exploiting this
vulnerability presents an opportunity for targeted intervention synthetic lethality
approaches. In this context, inhibiting a key survival DNA pathway becomes lethal upon
inhibition of a redundant pathway 9.

The synthetic lethal approach is particularly successful in targeting BRCA-and other HR-
deficient cancers 10, 11. Mutations in either BRCA1 or BRCA2 predispose individuals to the
development of breast or ovarian cancers, and approximately 10% of breast and 15% of
ovarian cancers are associated with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations. The BRCA1 and
BRCA2 proteins play crucial roles in HR, and DNA Rreplication fork protection, and ssDNA
gap suppression 3, 12. Mutations in these genes result in compelling tumor cells to rely on
alternative repair mechanisms which relies oNn PARP1-dependent ssDNA break/gap repair,
replication fork protection, translesion synthesis, or DSB repair 12-16. Inhibition of PARP1
in breast and ovarian cancers with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations results in significant cell
death in these tumors while Csparing normal cells 8. The approval of clinically used
PARP1/2-trapping inhibitors (commonly referred to as PARP inhibitors, PARPis), such as
Olaparib, Niraparib, RucRaparib, Veliparib, and Talazoparib, by the US FDA marks a pivotal
advancement of treatment for breast and ovarian cancers carrying BRCA mutations 12.
These inhibitors trap PARP1 at ssDNA breaks or gaps, inducing cell death in HR-deficient
cancer cells 17. However, despite the efficacy of those compounds, tumors often develop
resistance to PARPi 12, 18. This resistance can arise through various mechanisms,
including the restoration of HR including via secondary mutations or BRCA gene
reactivation, re-expression of BRCA expression, or inactivation of DNA damage sensor
proteins such as 53BP1. Additional resistance mechanisms include upregulation of
translesion synthesis and drug metabolism-related processes, such as enhanced drug
efflux 18. There are currently no effective treatment options for PARPi-resistant tumors,
and it is imperative to explore strategies for overcoming resistance to PARPi.

ATAD5 (also known as ELG1 in yeast) is an essential PCNA unloader that maintains
genome stability during DNA replication. Loss or depletion of ATAD5 results in persistent
PCNA retention on chromatin, replication fork stalling, and elevated replication stress,
ultimately contributing to genomic instability and tumorigenesis 19. Importantly, ATAD5-
luciferase expression of the reporter cell line is markedly induced under replication stress,
and this increase has been widely used as an established molecular marker for replication
stress responses 20. In 2010, we reported that a small molecule ML367 selectively
suppresses the elevation of ATAD5-luciferase protein levels in the reporter cell under
replication stress conditions 21.

We have exploited induction of the ATAD5 protein during replication stress as a marker
to screen for compounds that induce replication stress response 22-24. In the current study,
we identified ML367 and its derivative UNI418 as an inhibitory compound of replication
stress response and revealed that they inhibit PIKfRyve and PIP5K1C kinases, leading to
reduced cellular inositol hexaphosphate (IP ) levels and subsequent Cul4A-dependent
6
degradation of RAD51, CHK1 and CtIP, revNealing a mechanism of HR inhibition. We also
found that WDR5 is a DCAF protein of Cul4A determining substrate specificity of Cul4A
to RAD51 and CHK1. Due to the inhibition of key proteins for HR, gap repair, and DNA
replication stress response protCeins, UNI418 induced selective toxicity in PARP1-deficient
or PARPi-resistant cancer cells and tumors in xenograft models. We propose that this
pathway for regulating RHR by the phosphatidyl inositol signaling pathway may provide a
vulnerability for BRCA-deficient tumors.

## Results

Identification of a compound, UNI418 that inhibits DNA replication stress response
Our prior investigations revealed that ML367 functions as an inhibitor of the DNA
replication stress responses elicited by 5-fluorouridine (5-FUrd) 21. Subsequent screening

with enhanced efficacy in mitigating DNA replication stress. Among these derivatives,
UNI418 was identified as the most effective agent (Fig. 1a,b). The capacity of ML367 and
UNI418 to attenuate DNA replication stress was quantitaStively evaluated utilizing the
ATAD5-luciferase assay (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 1a). Notably, UNI418
suppressed the 5-FUrd-induced DNA replication stress response more potently than
ML367, as reflected by a lower IC
50

finding is supported by the observed reductions in phosphorylation of RPA32 at serine
residues S4 and S8, as well as CHK1, reIflecting the suppression of the DNA replication
stress response upon treatment witEh ML367 or UNI418 under DNA replication stress
conditions such as camptothecin (CPT), hydroxyurea (HU) and 5-FUrd (Fig. 1d,e and
Supplementary Fig. 1b). InteIrestingly, UNI418 treatment reduced the level of CHK1 as
well as its phosphorylation, even in the absence of DNA replication stress, suggesting it

I(1,3,4,5,6)P . Notably, IPMK has been implicated in the regulation of nuclear export of

of UNI418 for selectively targeting PARP1-

RAD51 following the completion of HR 6. To determine whether both RFWD3 and Cul4A
contribute to RAD51 proteolysis, we assessed RAD51 levels upon siRNA-mediated
depletion of RFWD3 (Supplementary Fig. 9g) and Cul4A, individually and in combination.
Silencing Cul4A resulted in increased RAD51 levels under both basal and IR-induced
conditions (Fig. 6d). In contrast, RFWD3 depletion led to RAD51 accumulation exclusively
in response to IR. Notably, co-silencing RFWD3 and Cul4A did not further augment
RAD51 levels beyond those observed upon individual knockdowns. These findings
suggest that Cul4A governs RAD51 homeostasis under normal physiological conditions,
whereas RFWD3 primarily mediates RAD51 degradation in response to DNA damage.

UNI418 inhibits tumor growth in PARP1-deficient tumors and enhances the efficacy
of PARPi in combination therapy
Building on the premise that UNI418's superior efficacy in killing PARP1-deficient cells
and its synergistic effect with PARPi in vitro (Fig. 3g,h,i,j) could translate into effective in
vivo antitumor activity, we conducted a series of tumor xenograft experiments. To this end,
we implanted either WT or PARP1-/- HCT116 cancer Scells into male NOD.CB17-
Prkdcscid/J mice to generate xenograft tumors. Upon the t S umors reaching an approximate
diameter of 0.5 cm, we administered 4 ml/kg of vehicle or 10 mg/kg of UNI418 directly
into the tumors every other day for a durationP of 12 days. Consistent with our initial
hypothesis, the application of UNI418 markedly suppressed tumor growth exclusively in
the PARP1-/- xenografts, with no significaInt effect observed in the WT tumors (Fig. 7a).
Notably, the co-administration of 50 mEg/kg Olaparib with 10 mg/kg UNI418 resulted in the
inhibition of HCT116 tumor growth, an outcome not achieved with either agent alone (Fig.
7b). Importantly, there was Ino significant alteration in the body weights of the mice
throughout the treatment period, irrespective of whether placebo or active drug treatment
was used (SupplemAentary Fig. 10a). The pharmacokinetic data of UNI418 was not yet
applicable for therapeutic use suggesting the need for further development for clinical
application (Supplementary Fig. 10b). These findings collectively underscore the potential
of UNI418, particularly in conjunction with Olaparib, as a promising therapeutic strategy
against cancers harboring PARP1 deficiencies and possibly extending to broader
applications in other tumor types.

UNI418 kills Olaparib-resistant ovarian cancer cells
Ovarian and breast tumors deficient in BRCA1 or BRCA2 are known to exhibit sensitivity
to PARPi such as Olaparib 8. Nonetheless, the therapeutic management of these
malignancies frequently culminates in the development of PARPi-resistant tumors, posing
a significant challenge to effective clinical outcomes. In this context, PEO-1 and Capan-1
cell lines, derived from BRCA2-deficient ovarian adenocarcinoma and pancreatic ductal
adenocarcinoma respectively, demonstrated susceptibility to PARPi treatment (Fig. 7c,f).
However, C4-2 and C2-2 clones, which originated from PEO-1 and Capan-1 cells,
respectively and harbor a reversion mutation in the BRCA2 gene, exhibited resistance to
PARPi, underscoring a pivotal mechanism of therapeutic evasion 44, 45. Given the
established selectivity of UNI418 for PARP1-/- cells (Fig. 3g,h), we posited that UNI418
might effectively target PARPi-resistant cancer cells, thereby re-sensitizing tumors that
have acquired resistance through BRCA2 reversion mutations to PARPi therapy. In
alignment with our hypothesis, the PARPi-resistant clones C4-2 and C2-2 displayed
enhanced sensitivity to UNI418 in comparison to their parental PEO-1 and Capan-1
counterparts (Fig. 7d,g). Moreover, co-administraEtion of UNI418 with Olaparib
significantly augmented the sensitivity of the PARPi-resistant C4-2 and C2-2 cells to
Olaparib, relative to treatment with Olaparib alone in the parental cell lines (Fig. 7e,h and
Supplementary Fig. 11). Crucially, this increase in drug sensitivity was paralleled by a
marked elevation in apoptotic cell death among the PARPi-resistant C4-2 cells following
UNI418 treatment (Fig. 7i). TheLse findings collectively suggest that UNI418 holds
considerable promise as a therapeutic agent capable of overcoming one of the common
pathways of acquired resisTtance to PARPi therapy of BRCA-deficient tumors.

In summary, our findings reveal that UNI418 exerts its effects by inhibiting PIKfyve and
PIP5K1C to reduce IP levels. This reduction in IP levels enhances Cul4A neddylation,
6 6
consequently activating the E3 ligase pathway. Activated Cul4A initiates the degradation
of HR proteins, ultimately leading to HR defects. In particular, the major recombinase
RAD51 and CHK1 are targeted by Cul4A with its specificity determined by a DCAF, WDR5.
Importantly, these HR defects render PARPi-resistant cells hypersensitive to UNI418
treatment. This comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying
UNI418's action provides valuable insights into its potential therapeutic applications for
treating PARPi-resistant cancers (Fig. 7j).

### Reviewer 2

In their study titled "Targeting IP6 signaling to destabilize homologous recombination proteins to overcome PARP inhibitor resistance” the authors present their findings demonstrating that targeting lipid kinases with the novel inhibitor UNI418 leads to a reduction in inositol hexaphosphate levels, in turn causing the degradation of homologous recombination proteins and a reduction in homologous recombination efficiency. This translates to a re-sensitization to PARP inhibitor in chemoresistance triple negative breast cancer cell lines. The data presented are generally convincing and I feel elucidate an interesting potential mechanism by which homologous recombination is regulated via proteasomal degradation signalled by inositol hexaphosphate levels. I have a few suggestions and concerns that I recommend be addressed to consolidate the work, and some comments to help improve the manuscript. 1. Data transparency – To facilitate data transparency, I suggest the authors show individual data points on all graphs so that readers get a better sense of the data distribution in experiments. 2. Western blot quantification – The authors mention several times that protein levels are significantly or substantially changed between different treatment conditions, but do not consistently present quantified data of relevant immunoblots supported with statistical tests to back up these otherwise only qualitative claims. I recommend that the authors include relevant quantifications of immunoblot data (where these claims are directed) to better support any assertions. The use of superlatives to describe changes should also be limited and/or fully removed, as these have limited quantitative meaning. 3. DNA Replication Stress Response – In figure 1, the authors measure DNA replication stress response suppression by induction of ATAD5. I am wondering how inhibition by the two small molecule inhibitors compares to inhibition of CHK1 phosphorylation via ATR inhibition, as that could be a good positive control for suppression of certain facets of the DNA replication stress response. 4. DNA replication stress response inhibition – Induction of ATAD5 between ML367 and UNI418 are different in figure 1C, making it difficult to make any comparison about suppression of DNA replication stress response as currently presented in the manuscript. Another interpretation could be that both inhibitors function similarly as they both result in ~75% reduction in signal at the highest concentration of inhibitor. Furthermore, the authors do not make any comparisons between dissociation constants or IC50 between ML367 and UNI418 in the text, which would allow readers to draw conclusions whether UNI418 displays heightened suppression of the DNA replication stress response. I suggest the authors make mention of these values to support their claims. 5. RAD51 Foci quantification in Figure 3 – please describe if this was done manually or whether an automated foci detection system was used. If the latter was used, please provide a brief description of the pipeline in the methods section. a. It is also important to understand whether cells in G2 phase were distinguished from cells in S-phase (at the time of irradiation / analysis of foci), as DSB repair processes between each phase are distinct. In the context of this work, selective analysis of cells irradiated in S-phase and analyzed in S-phase would be most logical. b. The legends indicate that these cells were monitored 1 hour after 10 Gy, a dose and time point that I am honestly very surprised that “only” an average of ~15 RAD51 foci are observed in the control / DMSO. From experience and understanding of comparable literature, foci numbers at least twice this are anticipated, as 10 Gy would be predicted to induce 100-200 DNA breaks in a G1 phase cell and 200-400 breaks in a G2 phase cell (with intermediate numbers in S-phase) depending on cell type genome content. While not all IR-induced breaks will undergo HR and form RAD51, at least 1/3 of induced breaks at any given time are expected to. It is not uncommon for radiation dosimetry here to vary substantially between groups if irradiator calibration is not up-to-date, or it could be possible that too many breaks are occurring and challenging for the authors to separate (foci are merging). I would advise the authors to examine this issue more closely in the context of what is understood from the published literature, as these numbers do appear far less than expected for that dose. c. Finally, while Figure 3B is helpful, it is a single time point and understanding whether the UNI418 specific effect is transient by performing a few timepoints in addition to the 1h would be helpful. 6. DSB Repair Efficiency – In figure 3F, the authors show both a large reduction in HR efficiency and a small reduction in NHEJ efficiency when cells are treated with UNI418 in the I-Sce1 plasmid reporter assay. Testing whether the repair of genomic breaks by monitoring foci numbers in G1, S, and G2 cells over a time course following some other form of genotoxic stress would further support the claims of reduced repair efficiency and validate the observations with the plasmid-based assay, which are otherwise not able to distinguish effects between phases. HU, IR, ATR inhibitors, Camptothecin, or even endogenous DNA replication stress might be used in this context – with the most important thing being to monitor damage formed and resolved in S-phase separately from other phases. 7. Synthetic lethality with Olaparib – it would be interesting to see how cell survival in the combination treatment compares to cell survival when BRCA1 or BRCA2 are knocked down by siRNA, as this is the canonical example of synthetic lethality in DNA repair. 8. PARPi resistance and re-sensitization – In Figure 7, the authors examine PARPi resistance by BRCA2 reversion, but there are quite a few known and different mechanisms that cells (especially cancer cells) can leverage to become more resistant to PARPi action. ### Reviewer 4

This manuscript by Dr. Myung’s group reports the identification and characterization of UNI418, a derivative of ML367, as an inhibitor of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C. The authors demonstrate that UNI418 inhibits the phosphatidyl inositol pathway, thereby activating the Cul4A–DDB1–WDR5 E3 ligase complex, which targets RAD51 and CHK1 for proteolysis. Consequently, UNI418 impairs HR, sensitizes tumor cells to PARP inhibitors, and overcomes PARPi resistance. I find this study both interesting and novel. The data are extensive and address the problem from multiple perspectives, making the manuscript potentially suitable for Nature Communications. I do not fundamentally disagree with the authors’ conclusions; however, I have several concerns regarding the interpretation and presentation of the results, as detailed below. I believe these points should be addressed to strengthen the manuscript. Introduction • The introduction should include the background of ATAD5. The authors state that ML367 was identified in 2010 and shown to increase ATAD5 protein levels under replication stress. Since UNI418 is a derivative of ML367, these facts, as well as the functional relevance of ATAD5 stabilization, should be included. Is it generally accepted that ATAD5 stabilization reflects replication stress? Figure 1 • The authors used 5-FU for 16–24 hours to induce replication stress. However, 5-FU is not a standard agent for inducing replication stress in cancer cells, and indeed pRPA32 was only modestly increased (Fig. 1d). Would similar results be obtained with other established replication stress inducers such as HU or camptothecin? • In Fig. 1d and e, the blot for total RPA2 should be shown. The CHK1 blot from Extended Data Fig. 1b could be moved to the main figure because it is the key point of Figure 1. • I recommend including supplementary data using alternative replication stress–inducing drugs to validate the conclusion that UNI418 represses replication stress. Figure 2 • Fig. 2a: The x-axis should be annotated. • Fig. 2d: The phosphatidylinositol pathway may be unfamiliar to many readers primarily interested in DNA damage responses and PARPi. A schematic explaining the relationships among PIKfyve, PI(3)P, PI(3,5)P2, and related molecules would be helpful. Figure 3 • Fig. 3a: The authors report that RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP are downregulated upon UNI418 treatment. However, RAD51 remains at a detectable level. o I strongly recommend performing a quantitative proteomic analysis to determine how many proteins are affected by UNI418. Is RAD51 one of a few or one of many targets? o The reduction in RAD51 should also be quantified from immunoblots and immunofluorescence (total levels, not just foci, if measurable). o Please also consider the literature: heterozygosity of key HR genes (RAD51, BRCA1/2) often does not produce strong phenotypes. For example, comparisons to RAD51+/- versus -/- (or BRCA1+/- vs. BRCA1-/-) cells can be found elsewhere. • Fig. 3b: A statistical analysis of UNI418 alone versus UNI418 + IR is warranted, as the remaining RAD51 foci formation appears different from the general BRCA1/2-deficient phenotype (no RAD51 foci formed). • Fig. 3c could be moved to Extended Data. • Fig. 3f: The reduction in HR frequency with UNI418 is much milder than with siRAD51. Please provide immunoblots of RAD51 under UNI418 and siRAD51 for comparison. • Fig. 3g: “parp1-/-” should be capitalized as “PARP1-/-” since it refers to the human gene knockout. • Fig. 3g and 3i: The authors used 0.25 μM UNI418, described as non-toxic to both cell types. If UNI418 is a catalytic inhibitor, why does its toxicity display clear dose dependence in PARP1-/- cells? Does RAD51 protein level also show dose-dependency by UNI418? o I am concerned that the apparent hypersensitivity of PARP1-/- cells by a dose-dependent UNI418 (1-5 uM >>0.25 uM) could reflect off-target effects, such as induction of PARP1-dependent DNA damage (base damage?). o Please include dose–response experiments (0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5 μM) to clarify this issue. Figure 4 • Fig. 4a: Since CHK1 is markedly reduced, its role in the drug sensitivity data must be considered. CHK1 inhibition is known to synergize with PARPi because PARPi-induced replication stress activates the ATR–CHK1 pathway. The authors should evaluate whether CHK1 suppression contributes to the observed olaparib sensitivity. • Fig. 4d: The sensitivity observed is mild (y-axis begins at 60%). HR-deficient cells are typically hypersensitive to olaparib at low micromolar or even nanomolar concentrations. o Please add control data for siBRCA1, siBRCA2, or siRAD51 cells for comparison. o The addition of UNI418 in these knockdown experiments (e.g., siPIKfyve + UNI418) would be informative. Figure 5 • Fig. 5a–b: The quantification is problematic. The Actin loading control is uneven, and the differences are marginal. Consider removing these panels if your conclusions remain supported without them. • Please illustrate a pathway for how excess IP6 diminishes Cul4A neddylation. • Fig. 5b: There is no additive effect of PIP5K1C knockdown and PIKfyve knockout, which appears inconsistent with Fig. 4d. Please discuss. • Fig. 5c: RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP levels increase under siCUL4A, but also under UNI418 treatment. The authors should provide an unbiased interpretation. Figure 6 • Fig. 6c: In siCtl cells, olaparib induces 20–40% cell death at 20–40 μM. Since the MOA of olaparib in HR-proficient cells is PARP trapping, these results need further explanation. How can siCUL4A or related treatments “rescue” HR-proficient cells? Excess RAD51 alone is unlikely to confer “super-HR” proficiency. Please consider alternative interpretations. Figure 7 • Fig. 7d, e, g, h: C4-2 and C2-2 cells (HR-proficient due to BRCA reversion mutations) are unexpectedly more sensitive to treatment. Please clarify why. • As the authors noted in the Introduction, the synthetic lethality between PARP deficiency and BRCA1/2 deficiency is commonly explained by ssDNA gap accumulation, fork reversal, and transcription–replication collisions. To reproduce these effects, genuine HR deficiency together with PARP catalytic inhibition is required. Importantly, PARP catalytic inhibition is fully achieved at concentrations below 1 μM olaparib. However, the data shown in Figure 7 demonstrate a dose-dependent effect of olaparib in the range of 1–10 μM, which is unlikely to reflect catalytic inhibition but rather PARP trapping. This makes the apparent effectiveness of the UNI418 and PARP-/- combination difficult to interpret. Given that the precise mechanism of action of PARP inhibitors, particularly in BRCA-deficient backgrounds, remains controversial, the authors should avoid attributing their findings solely to PARP inhibition. Additional testing with DNA-damaging agents such as camptothecin or cisplatin would help to substantiate whether the observed effects indeed arise from HR defects.

Foci were detected using the ZEN spot detection module with fixed thresholding parameters applied uniformly across all samples. Quantification was performed on ≥50 EdU-positive nuclei per condition. These details have been added to the Methods section. To address reviewer’s comment, we redid experiments several times more after recalibrating our x-ray machine. a. To address concerns regarding cell-cycle heterogeneity, we restricted our analysis to S-phase cells identified by EdU incorporation. Cells were pulse-labeled with EdU after irradiation, followed by Click-iT detection immediately prior to imaging. Only EdU-positive nuclei were included in the RAD51 foci quantification. This clarification has been added to Fig. 3b. b. b. In our repeated experiments, S-phase cells exhibited an average of more than 30 RAD51 foci at the 1 h time point. Reported values in the literature vary substantially depending on cell type, irradiation conditions, and quantification methods, ranging widely from ~20 to >80 foci. Therefore, the values observed in our experiments fall within the variability reported across published studies. c. In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we examined RAD51 foci at 1 h, 3 h, and 6 h after irradiation. The suppressive effect of UNI418 on RAD51 foci was observed at all timepoints, indicating that the effect is not transient. Comment 6: DSB Repair Efficiency – In figure 3F, the authors show both a large reduction in HR efficiency and a small reduction in NHEJ efficiency when cells are treated with UNI418 in the I-Sce1 plasmid reporter assay. Testing whether the repair of genomic breaks by monitoring foci numbers in G1, S, and G2 cells over a time course following some other form of genotoxic stress would further support the claims of reduced repair efficiency and validate the observations with the plasmid-based assay, which are otherwise not able to distinguish effects between phases. HU, IR, ATR inhibitors, Camptothecin, or even endogenous DNA replication stress might be used in this context – with the most important thing being to monitor damage formed and resolved in S-phase separately from other phases. Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion. We fully agree that monitoring DSB repair kinetics in G1, S, and G2 cells following genotoxic stress would provide additional mechanistic insight. However, performing a full cell-cycle–resolved time-course analysis using multiple markers (γH2AX, 53BP1, RAD51) is beyond the scope and technical feasibility of the current revision timeline. Importantly, our study already incorporates several complementary assays that directly assess HR repair efficiency in S-phase cells: • EdU-based RAD51 foci quantification (Fig. 3b), • I-SceI DR-GFP reporter assay (Fig. 3e), • Effects of UNI418 on replication-stress–induced DDR signaling (Fig. 1), all of which consistently demonstrate that UNI418 markedly reduces HR activity. While we agree that additional time-course experiments could provide further detail, the combined results from our existing assays robustly support the conclusion that UNI418 impairs HR-mediated DSB repair. Comment 7: Synthetic lethality with Olaparib – it would be interesting to see how cell survival in the combination treatment compares to cell survival when BRCA1 or BRCA2 are knocked down by siRNA, as this is the canonical example of synthetic lethality in DNA repair. Response: To address this point, we performed additional experiments using siBRCA2 as HR- deficient control (Fig. 4d). As expected, BRCA2 knockdown increased sensitivity to olaparib, serving as a canonical HR-deficient reference. Notably, the extent of viability reduction observed upon dual depletion of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C was comparable to that seen with BRCA2 knockdown. Comment 8: PARPi resistance and re-sensitization – In Figure 7, the authors examine PARPi resistance by BRCA2 reversion, but there are quite a few known and different mechanisms that cells (especially cancer cells) can leverage to become more resistant to PARPi action. It would be interesting to see whether BRCA1/2 negative cells that have restored homologous recombination repair due to TP53BP1 loss, or resistance due to increased efflux pump expression, are re-sensitized to PARPi when treated with UNI418. Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion. We fully agree that PARP inhibitor resistance can arise through multiple mechanisms, including TP53BP1 loss–mediated restoration of HR and drug efflux pump upregulation. Testing whether UNI418 re- sensitizes such models would indeed provide additional mechanistic insight. However, generating or obtaining TP53BP1-deficient BRCA1/2 mutant lines or efflux pump–overexpressing PARPi-resistant models, and validating their resistance mechanisms, is beyond the scope and technical feasibility of the current revision timeline. We will evaluate whether UNI418 could restore PARPi sensitivity to other types of resistant mechanisms in future study. Importantly, our study already demonstrates that UNI418 re-sensitizes PARPi-resistant cells driven by BRCA2 reversion, a clinically relevant resistance mechanism. Together with the consistent HR suppression shown in multiple independent assays (RAD51 foci, DR-GFP reporter, DDR signaling), our results strongly support the conclusion that UNI418 enhances PARPi sensitivity by targeting HR restoration. Comment 9: Big Picture – It is not clear within the discussion whether the authors think that their tool compounds can be modified for therapeutic purposes, and this would be helpful. I was also expecting some discussion about differences in IP and related biosynthetic 6 processes between normal and cancer cells, and between different cancer types that naturally would have plenty of metabolic variation given their context and specific genomic profile. Response: To address these points, we expanded the Discussion to incorporate broader therapeutic implications of UNI418 and to introduce biological differences in IP metabolism relevant 6 to cancer contexts. Specifically, we added a paragraph that discusses cancer-type– associated variation in IP biosynthetic enzymes and their potential influence on tumor 6 biology and treatment vulnerability: “In addition to these mechanistic findings, accumulating evidence suggests that IP6 metabolism itself may differ across cancer types. While UNI418 does not directly target IP6K or IPMK, dysregulation of these upstream enzymes has been associated with tumor biology and clinical prognosis. IP6K2 functions as a tumor suppressor in breast cancer, whereas IP6K1 upregulation correlates with aggressive recurrence and poor survival outcomes. These data suggest that distinct nodes within the inositol phosphate network are differentially exploited by malignancies. Tumors heavily dependent on HR and IP6 metabolic wiring may therefore be uniquely vulnerable to agents—such as UNI418—that reduce cellular IP pools. Future comparative metabolomic and genomic analyses across 6 tumor lineages will be essential for defining biomarkers that predict UNI418 sensitivity and guide clinical application. Taken together, these findings establish a mechanistic link between inositol phosphate signaling, HR dependency, and exploitable therapeutic vulnerabilities in DNA repair–dependent cancers, including those with BRCA dysfunction or PARPi resistance.” Comment 10: “DNA repair” – throughout this manuscript, the words “DNA repair” are used to actually refer to “DNA double strand break repair” or similar. The processes being discussed here are specific to that type of DNA damage in the context of DNA replication, and not all possible types of DNA damage that exist. Please amend all instances of that language to be specific. Response: Thanks for thoughtful comments. We fully agree that the term “DNA repair” was at times used in a broad manner, whereas the processes discussed in our study relate specifically to DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair mechanisms, particularly those occurring during DNA replication. To address this, we carefully revised the manuscript to ensure that terminology is used with appropriate specificity throughout. In all relevant sections—Introduction, Results, and Discussion—we replaced general references to “DNA repair” with more accurate terms such as “DNA double-strand break repair,” “DSB repair,” or “HR-dependent DSB repair,” depending on the context. Comment 11: Western blot loading control –In figure 1b, the appropriate loading control for pRPA32 is total RPA32 levels, please include this control. H3 is less ideal in the context of that experiment. Response: We agree that total RPA32 serves as a more appropriate loading control for pRPA32 analysis. To address the reviewer’s request, we additionally treated cells with CPT and HU and examined CHK1, p-CHK1, p-RPA32, and total RPA32 levels. The results indicate that CHK1, p-CHK1, and p-RPA32 were reduced in ML367-treated cells and further decreased upon UNI418 treatment, whereas total RPA32 levels remained unchanged (Fig 1d, 1e). In Extended Fig. 1b, we showed that 5-FUrd treatment decreased p- CHK1 and CHK1 in ML367-treated cells and further reduced p-CHK1 and CHK1 in UNI418-treated cells. Comment 12: How these inhibitors are referred to – generally it is advisable to be specific and call them PARP1/2-trapping inhibitors, as other small molecules that block PARP enzyme action exist, with no to variable impact on trapping PARP enzymes at sites of DNA leading to damage. Response: We agree that the term “PARP inhibitors” can be ambiguous, as it encompasses both catalytic inhibitors and clinically used agents that induce PARP1/2 trapping. To address this, the sentence in the Introduction has been updated to: “The approval of clinically used PARP1/2-trapping inhibitors (commonly referred to as PARP inhibitors, PARPis), such as Olaparib, Niraparib, Rucaparib, Veliparib, and Talazoparib, by the US FDA, marks a pivotal advancement in the treatment of breast and ovarian cancers carrying BRCA mutations.” We have applied this terminology consistently throughout the revised manuscript. Comment 13: Data normalization –In Figure 1a, it is not clearly stated whether the Luc-ATAD5 data is normalized or not. The authors should revise all figures and clearly state whether the data is normalized, and if so, what the data is normalized to. Response: In Figure 1a, the Luc-ATAD5 activity was normalized to the NT (non-treated) control, which was set to 1, and all other values are presented as relative fold changes. We have now clarified this in the figure legend. We also carefully reviewed other figures and added explicit descriptions of normalization methods in the corresponding legends wherever necessary to ensure consistency and transparency in data presentation. Comment 14: Phosphorylation of CHK1 – I would suggest including the blot of phospho-CHK1 in the main body of the manuscript in figure 1. Response: In accordance with the comment, we have moved the phospho-CHK1 blot into the main Figure 1d. Additionally, based on comments from other reviewers, we repeated the experiments under multiple conditions, including ATR inhibitor treatment, to more comprehensively assess CHK1 phosphorylation dynamics. The revised figure now reflects these updated and expanded datasets. Comment 15: Kinase screen – I suggest the authors include extended data figure 2 in the main body as it guides the narrative of the study. I would also ask for more details on what precent control is referring to, and that the authors label the kinases of interest within the plot to make it more clear to the reader. Therefore, instead of labeling them within the plot, we have listed the names of the 22 kinases (0–10% control group) below the figure for clarity. Response: In the revised manuscript, we regenerated the graph using Prism to improve overall clarity and readability and added the appropriate axis labels. The updated graph is now presented as Fig. 2b. Comment 17: Surface plasmon resonance – In figure 2B, there is no description of what the black lines underneath the colored lines represent. Please include this information within the appropriate figure legends. Comment 20: CUL4A neddylation – Figure 5a and 5b are missing a control that clearly demonstrates that the higher molecular weight CUL4A band is clearly CUL4A-Nedd. These changes have been incorporated into the revised figure (now included in Extended Data Fig. 9c). Comment 22: IPPK siRNA – The authors did not include a control demonstrating the effectiveness of their siRNA against IPPK. Response: To address this concern, we performed RT–qPCR analysis to evaluate the knockdown efficiency of IPPK following siRNA treatment. The results confirming effective depletion of IPPK mRNA have been added to the revised manuscript (now included in Extended Data Fig. 9f). Comment 23: In figure 6C, the authors make the claim that silencing WDR or CUL4A causes resistance to Olaparib, but only shows comparison compared to vehicle controls. To support this claim, please show the results of the statistical test between the different siRNAs at 20 µM and 40 µM Olaparib.
