The updated statistical analyses are now reflected in the revised Fig. 6c, and the corresponding significance values have been added to the figure. Reviewer #3 and #4 Comment 1: The introduction should include the background of ATAD5. The authors state that ML367 was identified in 2010 and shown to increase ATAD5 protein levels under replication stress. Since UNI418 is a derivative of ML367, these facts, as well as the functional relevance of ATAD5 stabilization, should be included. Is it generally accepted that ATAD5 stabilization reflects replication stress? Response: In response, we have revised the Introduction to include background information regarding ATAD5 biology, its relevance to replication stress, and the historical connection between ML367 and UNI418. Specifically, we added the following paragraph to provide conceptual context: “ATAD5 (also known as ELG1 in yeast) is an essential PCNA unloader that maintains genome stability during DNA replication. Loss or depletion of ATAD5 results in persistent PCNA retention on chromatin, replication fork stalling, and elevated replication stress, ultimately contributing to genomic instability and tumorigenesis 19. Importantly, ATAD5- luciferase expression of the reporter cell line is markedly induced under replication stress, and this increase has been widely used as an established molecular marker for replication stress responses 20. In 2010, we reported that a small molecule ML367 selectively suppresses the elevation of ATAD5-luciferase protein levels in the reporter cell under replication stress conditions 21.” Comment 2: • The authors used 5-FU for 16–24 hours to induce replication stress. However, 5-FU is not a standard agent for inducing replication stress in cancer cells, and indeed pRPA32 was only modestly increased (Fig. 1d). Would similar results be obtained with other established replication stress inducers such as HU or camptothecin? • I recommend including supplementary data using alternative replication stress– inducing drugs to validate the conclusion that UNI418 represses replication stress. Response: We agree that 5-FUrd is not the most commonly used replication stress inducer and understand the reviewer’s concern regarding p-RPA32 signal intensity. In response, we performed additional experiments using two well-established replication stress agents, hydroxyurea (HU) and camptothecin (CPT). Cells were treated with HU or CPT, followed by ML367 or UNI418 exposure, and we examined CHK1, p-CHK1, p-RPA32, and total RPA32 levels. Consistent with our original 5-FUrd data, HU and CPT treatment revealed that CHK1, p-CHK1, and p-RPA32 were reduced by ML367 and further decreased by UNI418, while total RPA32 remained unchanged. These results confirm that UNI418 suppresses replication stress signaling across multiple replication-blocking agents. The newly obtained HU and CPT data have been incorporated as Fig. 1d and 1e in the revised manuscript. Comment 3: • In Fig. 1d and e, the blot for total RPA2 should be shown. The CHK1 blot from Extended Data Fig. 1b could be moved to the main figure because it is the key point of Figure 1. Response: Thanks for the suggestion. Fig. 1d and 1e are now presented with newly generated HU- and CPT-based replication stress experiments, and these panels include total RPA32 blots to provide appropriate loading controls. Regarding the CHK1 and p-CHK1 results originally shown in Extended Data Fig. 1b under 5-FUrd treatment, we retained these data in the extended section because HU and CPT experiments now occupy the corresponding position in the main figure panels. Therefore, the expanded CHK1 and p-CHK1 blots under 5-FUrd treatment are presented in the updated Extended Data Figure, while Figures 1d and 1e in the main manuscript focus on HU and CPT-based stress responses. Comment 4: • Fig. 2a: The x-axis should be annotated. Response: Sorry not to provide better graph in the original submission. We have improved the quality of Fig 2d (now Fig. 2b) by replacing the original graph which was provided by the company with a newly generated version using GraphPad Prism with actual dataset, which now includes clear X- and Y-axis labels, error ranges and higher graphical clarity. Comment 5: • Fig. 2d: The phosphatidylinositol pathway may be unfamiliar to many readers primarily interested in DNA damage responses and PARPi. A schematic explaining the relationships among PIKfyve, PI(3)P, PI(3,5)P2, and related molecules would be helpful. Response: To address this, we have added a schematic diagram illustrating the enzymatic relationships among PIKfyve, PI(3)P, PI(3,5)P₂, and related inositol phosphates. This schematic has been incorporated into the revised Fig. 2e to aid understanding of how UNI418 interacts with lipid kinase signaling pathways. Comment 6: • Fig. 3a: The authors report that RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP are downregulated upon UNI418 treatment. However, RAD51 remains at a detectable level. o I strongly recommend performing a quantitative proteomic analysis to determine how many proteins are affected by UNI418. Is RAD51 one of a few or one of many targets? Response: To address whether UNI418 broadly affects the proteome or selectively targets specific proteins, we conducted SILAC-based quantitative mass spectrometry in an independent validation experiment. The analysis indicated that UNI418 does not cause global protein degradation but instead affects a restricted subset of proteins. Notably, several replication-associated and chromatin-regulatory proteins, including MCM2, MCM5, MCM6, MCM7, and UHRF1, were consistently reduced upon UNI418 treatment. In contrast, RAD51 was not quantified in this dataset due to insufficient peptide coverage, likely reflecting low abundance and technical limitations of the LC–MS/MS run rather than lack of biological regulation. These results support our conclusion that UNI418 does not induce nonspecific proteolysis but instead modulates a defined set of proteins linked to DNA replication and genome stability. Because these SILAC data were performed as supportive validation and are not essential for the central conclusions of the manuscript, we did not include them in the revised figures. Nevertheless, we are happy to provide the data to the editor or reviewers upon request. Furthermore, we plan to reveal other proteins targeted by UNI418 using WDR5 interacting protein upon UNI418 treatment under proteasome inhibition. However, due to time limit for revision, constructing WDR5-BioID with inducible manner was not feasible. We plan to explore this direction in future. Comment 7: o The reduction in RAD51 should also be quantified from immunoblots and immunofluorescence (total levels, not just foci, if measurable). Response: As recommended, we performed quantitative analysis of RAD51 protein levels: - Western blot band intensities were quantified using ImageJ across ≥3 independent experiments. - RAD51 immunofluorescence (total nuclear signal, not only foci) was quantified using ZEN software. Both analyses consistently show a significant reduction in RAD51 upon UNI418 treatment. These quantifications have been added to the revised Fig. 3b and corresponding Extended Data Fig. 6b. Comment 8: o Please also consider the literature: heterozygosity of key HR genes (RAD51, BRCA1/2) often does not produce strong phenotypes. For example, comparisons to RAD51+/- versus -/- (or BRCA1+/- vs. BRCA1-/-) cells can be found elsewhere. Response: We have included additional discussion comparing our findings to known RAD51+/− and BRCA1+/− phenotypes. We believe that partial reduction rather than complete loss of RAD51 protein following UNI418 treatment causes mild but significant HR defect due to: - concurrent degradation of multiple HR regulators (RAD51, CHK1, CtIP), - UNI418 reduces RAD51 little more than half compared to RAD51+/-, - Cul4A activation amplifying proteolysis, - the requirement for precise stoichiometry in HR machinery. This explanation has been added in the Discussion to contextualize the observed phenotype. Comment 9: • Fig. 3b: A statistical analysis of UNI418 alone versus UNI418 + IR is warranted, as the remaining RAD51 foci formation appears different from the general BRCA1/2-deficient phenotype (no RAD51 foci formed). Response: As requested, we performed statistical analysis comparing the control, UNI418, IR, and UNI418 + IR conditions. Quantification of RAD51 foci in EdU-positive nuclei showed: - Control: ~6 foci - UNI418 alone: ~4 foci - IR (1 h): ~30 foci - UNI418 + IR (1 h): ~14 foci These analyses confirm that IR induces robust RAD51 foci formation, and that UNI418 reduces the number of IR-induced foci to an intermediate level. Statistical comparisons have been added to the revised figure, and the manuscript text has been updated accordingly. Comment 10: • Fig. 3c could be moved to Extended Data. Response: In accordance with this recommendation, Figure 3c has been moved to Extended Data Fig. 6c in the revised manuscript. Comment 11: • Fig. 3f: The reduction in HR frequency with UNI418 is much milder than with siRAD51. Please provide immunoblots of RAD51 under UNI418 and siRAD51 for comparison. Response: As requested, we have provided immunoblots comparing RAD51 protein levels under UNI418 treatment and siRAD51 knockdown, now included in Extended Data Fig. 7c. Consistent with the observed differences in HR frequency, siRAD51 almost completely depleted RAD51 protein, whereas UNI418 treatment resulted in a partial reduction, leaving a detectable residual level of RAD51. This difference in RAD51 depletion efficiency explains why the reduction in HR frequency by UNI418 appears milder than that observed with siRAD51. Comment 12: • Fig. 3g: “parp1-/-” should be capitalized as “PARP1-/-” since it refers to the human gene knockout. Response: Thanks for the comment. The notation has been corrected from parp1-/- to PARP1-/- throughout the manuscript, including in Figure 3g. Comment 13: • Fig. 3g and 3i: The authors used 0.25 µM UNI418, described as non-toxic to both cell types. If UNI418 is a catalytic inhibitor, why does its toxicity display clear dose dependence in PARP1-/- cells? Does RAD51 protein level also show dose-dependency by UNI418? o I am concerned that the apparent hypersensitivity of PARP1-/- cells by a dose-dependent UNI418 (1-5 uM >>0.25 uM) could reflect off-target effects, such as induction of PARP1-dependent DNA damage (base damage?). o Please include dose–response experiments (0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5 µM) to clarify this issue. Response: To address the concern, we performed dose–response analyses of UNI418 (0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5 µM) in both HCT116 WT and HCT116 PARP1-/- cells and examined RAD51, CHK1, CtIP, CUL4A, and γH2AX levels by immunoblotting (now included in Extended Data Fig. 8a). RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP showed a clear dose-dependent reduction in both WT and PARP1-/- cells. This pattern is consistent with our model in which UNI418 inhibits PIKfyve/PIP5K1C, decreases IP levels, and enhances Cul4A-mediated proteolysis of HR 6 factors. Importantly, the reduction is gradual rather than abrupt or irregular, which does not support an off-target toxicity effect. A dose-dependent increase in γH2AX was observed in PARP1-/- cells, and the magnitude was significantly higher than in WT cells. This heightened sensitivity is expected because PARP1-/- cells rely more heavily on HR to resolve replication-associated DNA damage; therefore, additional UNI418-mediated suppression of HR proteins leads to greater accumulation of DNA breaks. Together, these results support that the hypersensitivity of PARP1-/- cells reflects their increased dependence on HR rather than off-target toxicity of UNI418. Comment 14: • Fig. 4a: Since CHK1 is markedly reduced, its role in the drug sensitivity data must be considered. CHK1 inhibition is known to synergize with PARPi because PARPi-induced replication stress activates the ATR–CHK1 pathway. The authors should evaluate whether CHK1 suppression contributes to the observed olaparib sensitivity. Response: We agree with the reviewer that CHK1 plays a critical role in the cellular response to replication stress and that pharmacological or genetic suppression of CHK1 has been reported to synergize with PARP inhibition. PARPi-induced replication stress activates the ATR–CHK1 signaling axis, and inhibition of CHK1 compromises S-phase checkpoint control, leading to replication fork collapse and enhanced cytotoxicity. In our study, UNI418 treatment leads to a reduction in CHK1 protein levels concomitant with depletion of other HR-associated factors, including RAD51 and CtIP (Fig. 4a,b). We therefore acknowledge that CHK1 suppression is likely to contribute to the enhanced sensitivity to olaparib observed upon UNI418 treatment. However, several lines of evidence suggest that this effect cannot be attributed solely to CHK1 loss. First, UNI418 induces concurrent destabilization of multiple HR regulators rather than selectively targeting CHK1. Second, UNI418 markedly suppresses RAD51 foci formation and HR reporter activity, indicating a direct impairment of homologous recombination capacity. Third, the absence of additive effects between UNI418 treatment and genetic depletion of PIKfyve/PIP5K1C supports a shared upstream mechanism involving IP -dependent 6 Cul4A activation rather than isolated checkpoint inhibition. Taken together, our findings are consistent with a model in which UNI418-induced CHK1 reduction contributes to olaparib sensitivity as part of a broader HR-defective state, rather than acting as the sole driver of drug synergy. We have revised the Discussion to explicitly acknowledge the contribution of CHK1 suppression and to contextualize our results within the established ATR–CHK1–PARP interaction framework. Comment 15: • Fig. 4d: The sensitivity observed is mild (y-axis begins at 60%). HR-deficient cells are typically hypersensitive to olaparib at low micromolar or even nanomolar concentrations. o Please add control data for siBRCA1, siBRCA2, or siRAD51 cells for comparison. o The addition of UNI418 in these knockdown experiments (e.g., siPIKfyve + UNI418) would be informative. Response: To address this point, we performed additional experiments using siBRCA2 as HR- deficient control (Fig. 4d). As expected, BRCA2 knockdown increased sensitivity to olaparib, serving as a canonical HR-deficient reference. Notably, the extent of viability reduction observed upon dual depletion of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C was comparable to that seen with BRCA2 knockdown. We also examined whether UNI418 further enhances sensitivity when combined with siPIKfyve, siPIP5K1C, or the double knockdown (Fig. 4d). Interestingly, UNI418 treatment alone reduced viability to a similar extent, and additional knockdown of PIKfyve, PIP5K1C, or both did not further sensitize cells beyond the effect of UNI418 alone. These results suggest that the sensitizing effect of UNI418 and the combined depletion of PIKfyve/PIP5K1C converge on the same pathway, reflecting a shared mechanism involving decreased IP and consequent reduction of HR protein stability. 6 Comment 16: • Fig. 5a–b: The quantification is problematic. The Actin loading control is uneven, and the differences are marginal. Consider removing these panels if your conclusions remain supported without them. Response: In response to this concern—and consistent with similar comments from other reviewers—we repeated the experiments in Fig. 5a, including three independent biological replicates, and replaced the original panels with newly generated data. To verify that the upper CUL4A band represents the neddylated form, we additionally included MLN4924, a well-characterized neddylation inhibitor. As expected, MLN4924 treatment eliminated the upper band, confirming its identity as CUL4A–Nedd. Furthermore, we optimized sample loading and exposure conditions to ensure uniform Actin loading controls and clearer quantification across all replicates. The updated blots and quantification now show a consistent and reproducible reduction in CUL4A neddylation upon UNI418 treatment. Thus, with the improved data quality and proper validation using MLN4924, we believe these panels provide meaningful mechanistic support and have retained them in the revised manuscript. Comment 17: Please illustrate a pathway for how excess IP6 diminishes Cul4A neddylation Response: To address this point, we have revised the hypothetical model presented in Fig. 7j. Accordingly, we have added the following description to the figure legend of Fig. 7j: “Lipid kinases, such as PIKfyve and PIP5K1C, regulate cellular IP6 levels through the phosphatidylinositol signaling pathway. IP6 suppresses Cul4A ubiquitin ligase activity by promoting its deneddylation (N8) by the COP9 signalosome (CSN), thereby stabilizing key HR proteins such as RAD51 and CHK1.” Comment 18: • Fig. 5b: There is no additive effect of PIP5K1C knockdown and PIKfyve knockout, which appears inconsistent with Fig. 4d. Please discuss. Response: Although double depletion of PIKfyve and PIP5K1C results in a stronger reduction in cell viability compared to the single knockdowns (Fig. 4d), this additive effect is not reflected at the level of CUL4A neddylation (Fig. 5b). There are several biological reasons why these observations are not inconsistent. First, CUL4A neddylation appears to behave as a threshold- or saturation-type response. Our data indicate that knockdown of either PIKfyve or PIP5K1C alone is already sufficient to reduce IP6 to a level that maximally triggers CUL4A de-neddylation. As such, additional depletion of the second kinase may not further increase the magnitude of this biochemical readout. In contrast, cell viability represents a downstream, cumulative phenotype that integrates multiple layers of replication stress and impaired HR repair. Therefore, even if CUL4A de- neddylation does not further decrease beyond a threshold, the combined depletion of both kinases exacerbates cellular stress and leads to a more pronounced loss of viability. Taken together, the absence of an additive effect in CUL4A neddylation is consistent with a saturable mechanistic response upstream, whereas the stronger viability defect reflects downstream amplification of replication stress and HR deficiency. We have added this explanation to the revised manuscript. Comment 19: • Fig. 5c: RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP levels increase under siCUL4A, but also under UNI418 treatment. The authors should provide an unbiased interpretation. Response: We agree that the interpretation of Fig. 5c should be clearly described. siCUL4A alone increases RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP levels compared with control (C), consistent with the role of CUL4A as an E3 ligase promoting proteolysis of these proteins. UNI418 alone decreases RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP levels compared with control, in line with our model that UNI418 enhances Cul4A-dependent degradation of HR factors. When UNI418 and siCUL4A are combined, HR protein levels are elevated compared with UNI418 alone but do not fully return to the siCUL4A-only levels. We interpret this partial rescue as a consequence of incomplete depletion of CUL4A protein by siRNA treatment. Consistent with many E3 ligases, even modest residual amounts of CUL4A can retain biological activity. Thus, partial knockdown likely limits the extent to which CUL4A- dependent proteolysis can be fully suppressed, resulting in an incomplete recovery of HR protein levels under UNI418 treatment. Comment 20: • Fig. 6c: In siCtl cells, olaparib induces 20–40% cell death at 20–40 µM. Since the MOA of olaparib in HR-proficient cells is PARP trapping, these results need further explanation. How can siCUL4A or related treatments “rescue” HR-proficient cells? Excess RAD51 alone is unlikely to confer “super-HR” proficiency. Please consider alternative interpretations. Response: We note that olaparib can induce measurable cell death even in HR-proficient cells due to PARP1 trapping. The 20–40% decrease in viability in siCtrl cells at 20–40 µM olaparib is therefore consistent with the well-established cytotoxicity of PARP-trapping lesions in otherwise HR-competent cells. Importantly, the apparent “rescue” observed in siCUL4A cells should not be interpreted as enhanced HR capacity (“super-HR”). Instead, our data suggests an alternative explanation: CUL4A depletion partially alleviates replication-associated stress that is exacerbated by PARP trapping. Because CUL4A promotes proteolysis of several replication- and repair- associated proteins, its knockdown increases steady-state levels of multiple factors involved in maintaining replication fork stability. This general increase in replication- supporting proteins likely provides a modest buffering effect against PARP-trapping– induced stress, resulting in slightly improved survival relative to siCtrl. Thus, the reduced sensitivity to olaparib in siCUL4A cells does not reflect enhanced HR per se, but rather a broader dampening of replication stress via reduced CUL4A- mediated proteolysis. We have revised the manuscript to clarify this interpretation and avoid overstatement of HR dependence. Comment 21: • Fig. 7d, e, g, h: C4-2 and C2-2 cells (HR-proficient due to BRCA reversion mutations) are unexpectedly more sensitive to treatment. Please clarify why. Response: Although C4-2 and C2-2 cells restore BRCA2 function through reversion mutations and are categorized as HR-proficient, multiple studies have shown that BRCA-reverted cancer cells do not fully regain the genomic stability of genuinely HR-proficient cells. Instead, they retain elevated levels of replication stress and persistent genomic instability due to accumulated mutations and chromosomal rearrangements that arise prior to reversion. As a consequence, BRCA-reverted tumor cells remain highly dependent on robust HR and replication-stress response pathways for survival. Because UNI418 induces Cul4A-mediated degradation of essential HR factors—including RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP—the HR capacity of BRCA-reverted cells is disproportionately compromised upon UNI418 treatment. This heightened reliance on HR makes C4-2 and C2-2 cells more vulnerable to UNI418 compared with their parental BRCA2-deficient PEO-1 and Capan-1 cells. Consistent with this interpretation, UNI418 treatment led to a marked increase in apoptotic cell death specifically in C4-2 cells (Fig. 7i). This mechanistic vulnerability also explains why the combination of UNI418 and Olaparib produced stronger synthetic lethality in BRCA-reverted cells relative to parental lines. We have included this explanation in the revised manuscript. Comment 22: • As the authors noted in the Introduction, the synthetic lethality between PARP deficiency and BRCA1/2 deficiency is commonly explained by ssDNA gap accumulation, fork reversal, and transcription–replication collisions. To reproduce these effects, genuine HR deficiency together with PARP catalytic inhibition is required. Importantly, PARP catalytic inhibition is fully achieved at concentrations below 1 µM olaparib. However, the data shown in Figure 7 demonstrate a dose-dependent effect of olaparib in the range of 1–10 µM, which is unlikely to reflect catalytic inhibition but rather PARP trapping. This makes the apparent effectiveness of the UNI418 and PARP-/- combination difficult to interpret. Given that the precise mechanism of action of PARP inhibitors, particularly in BRCA-deficient backgrounds, remains controversial, the authors should avoid attributing their findings solely to PARP inhibition. Additional testing with DNA-damaging agents such as camptothecin or cisplatin would help to substantiate whether the observed effects indeed arise from HR defects. Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s detailed mechanistic insight. We agree that PARP catalytic inhibition is largely saturated at concentrations below 1 µM olaparib, and therefore the dose-dependent effects observed at 1–10 µM in Fig. 7 primarily reflect PARP–DNA trapping activity rather than catalytic inhibition alone. In the revised manuscript, we have clarified that the observed synthetic lethality between UNI418 and olaparib should not be interpreted exclusively through catalytic inhibition mechanisms. Importantly, our central conclusion—that UNI418 restores vulnerability in PARPi-resistant or BRCA-reverted cells by compromising HR capacity—does not rely solely on PARP inhibition. Multiple independent lines of evidence support HR impairment by UNI418: - UNI418 drives Cul4A-dependent degradation of RAD51, CHK1, and CtIP, leading to HR factor depletion (Fig. 3a; Extended Fig. 6). - RAD51 foci formation after IR is strongly suppressed by UNI418, particularly in S-phase cells (Fig. 3b). - HR reporter assays confirm significant loss of HR activity following UNI418 treatment (Fig. 3e). - UNI418 enhances γH2AX accumulation in PARP1–/– cells, consistent with increased DSB burden in HR-defective backgrounds (Extended Fig. 8a). In addition, to address the reviewer’s concern about whether UNI418-induced cellular responses extend beyond olaparib-specific contexts, we performed biochemical validation using alternative replication stress inducers. CPT or HU treatment revealed that CHK1, p-CHK1, and p-RPA32 levels decreased with ML367 and were further reduced with UNI418, while total RPA32 remained unchanged (Fig. 1d and e). These findings demonstrate that UNI418 suppresses replication stress signaling independent of PARP inhibitor exposure, further supporting our HR-defect model. Although we did not extend CPT or cisplatin experiments to full viability assays, we believe that the combined biochemical and functional data—spanning protein stability, RAD51 dynamics, foci formation, HR reporter output, and replication stress signaling—provide a strong mechanistic foundation for attributing UNI418 efficacy to HR pathway disruption rather than PARP-specific responses. Reviewer #4 We thank the reviewer for this important comment regarding the interpretation of Fig. 4d and the strength of olaparib sensitivity in BRCA2-depleted cells. We agree that the degree of sensitivity observed in the original CellTiter-Glo assay (72- hour treatment) appeared modest compared to the well-established hypersensitivity of bona fide BRCA2-deficient cells to PARP inhibitors. We note that the original experiment measured short-term metabolic viability after 3 days of drug exposure, which can underestimate long-term clonogenic cell death and primarily reflects proliferation and metabolic activity rather than sustained survival. To directly address this concern, we performed additional clonogenic survival assays using siBRCA2-treated cells under prolonged olaparib exposure (7-day growth). Under these conditions, BRCA2 knockdown cells showed strong hypersensitivity to olaparib, with more than 50% reduction in colony formation even at low olaparib concentrations, consistent with canonical HR-deficient responses to PARP inhibition. These new clonogenic data are now provided in Extended Data Fig. 8d. We have revised the manuscript to clarify the differences between the CellTiter-Glo viability assay and the clonogenic survival assay and to note that the clonogenic data confirm robust Olaparib hypersensitivity in BRCA2-depleted cells.
